lessons.title: Revise a message for its reader and purpose.
lessons.body: The reader needs enough information to act. Name the problem, the help needed and a useful time. Replace vague words such as it, soon and broken when their meaning is unclear.
lessons.example: A confirmed Tuesday meeting at 2 pm has moved to 3 pm in the same room.
steps: Name Tuesday’s meeting so readers know which plan changed.
State 3 pm replaces 2 pm, with the same room.
Check that every affected reader receives the confirmed update.
lessons.whyItWorks: Revision begins with purpose and audience. Ask what the reader must understand or do, then change the content and order to support that purpose. Editing spelling is useful, but it comes after deciding whether the right information is present. Read a draft from the receiver’s position, including what they do not already know.
lessons.watchFor: A longer or more formal replacement can be less clear than the original.

lessons.title: Use a two-pass check
lessons.body: Revision changes meaning, order or detail to help the reader. Check facts and the purpose before polishing spelling. Keep only the personal information the task needs.
lessons.example: Work through the reasoning
steps: Content: are the date, time, place, and request correct?
Clarity: can pronouns or vague words confuse the reader?
Proofread the final version after larger changes are made.
lessons.whyItWorks: Revise one kind of problem at a time: missing information, unclear references, organization, then sentence details. Compare the before and after versions and name what improved. Keeping both versions makes revision visible and shows that a first draft is material to work with, not a permanent verdict on your ability.
lessons.watchFor: Do not remove a condition or exception just to make a sentence shorter.

units.title: Look behind an argument
units.goal: Find the proposal, its evidence and a fair objection.
units.why: Identify a claim, its reasons, and its limits.

lessons.title: Identify a claim, its reasons, and its limits.
lessons.body: An argument connects a proposal with reasons and evidence. Find what the writer wants to happen. Then ask which facts support that choice.
lessons.example: “Keep the library open later: evening visits increased during the trial.”
steps: Claim: keep later opening hours.
Evidence: evening visits increased during the trial.
Missing detail: how much, over what period, and at what staffing cost?
lessons.whyItWorks: An argument has a claim, reasons, and an implied link between them. Ask whether accepting the evidence would make the conclusion more reasonable. Then identify what else would need to be true. More visitors during a trial might support longer opening hours, but the argument may still need information about costs and whether the pattern continued.
lessons.watchFor: Strong emotion can show importance without proving a factual claim.

lessons.title: Test assumptions and counterarguments
lessons.body: A fair objection points out a cost, risk or missing detail. Answering it makes the proposal stronger. Attacking the person does not answer their concern.
lessons.example: Work through the reasoning
steps: Later visits alone do not tell us whether the added hours are affordable.
Compare additional use with staffing needs.
A limited trial may be a better-supported proposal than a permanent change immediately.
lessons.whyItWorks: A counterargument targets a relevant weakness, not the person making the argument. Consider whether an objection changes your conclusion or simply limits it. A narrower proposal can be better supported: a longer trial may fit uncertain evidence better than a permanent change. Explain why you accept one option while acknowledging its tradeoffs.
lessons.watchFor: Repeating the conclusion in different words does not supply evidence.

review: An argument connects a proposal with reasons and evidence. Find what the writer wants to happen. Then ask which facts support that choice.

lessons.title: Give a work message a clear purpose
lessons.body: Put the main point early. Say what is finished, what is not, and what you need. Keep a confirmed fact separate from an estimate.
lessons.example: Eight of nine boxes are packed. One box is missing; delivery is due at 3 pm.
steps: State the job and progress: eight of nine boxes are packed.
Name the blocker: the last box is missing.
Ask whether a replacement box can be provided before the 3 pm delivery.
lessons.whyItWorks: Work messages should make the next action clear. Put the topic and main point early, include the relevant date or task, and state any action requested. Match tone to the situation while staying direct. A useful subject line helps the receiver recognize the message without opening several unrelated conversations.
lessons.watchFor: Politeness does not require hiding the actual request.

lessons.title: Revise before sending
lessons.body: If the first plan cannot happen, offer a realistic alternative. Name who needs to decide. Do not promise a result that depends on an unconfirmed step.
lessons.example: A missing box can arrive only at 3:30 pm, after the 3 pm delivery deadline.
steps: State what changed and its effect on the delivery.
Offer a workable option: send eight now and the last later, if the supervisor agrees.
Ask for the priority and record the confirmed decision. Do not promise an unagreed split delivery.
lessons.whyItWorks: Before sending, check recipients, attachments, names, dates, and whether the wording commits you to something you can actually do. Describe a problem using facts and a proposed next step. If an instruction is unclear or conflicting, ask for clarification instead of inventing a promise. Keep private information out unless the recipient needs it.
lessons.watchFor: A confident promise is not useful if the deadline or responsibility was never confirmed.

units.goal: Find the original record and check what it can tell you.
units.why: Find, evaluate, and acknowledge a useful source.

lessons.title: Find, evaluate, and acknowledge a useful source.
lessons.body: Trace a claim to the original record, not just its repetitions. Check the creator, date, place and method. Two articles repeating one survey provide one underlying survey, not two independent studies.
lessons.example: Question: when does the community centre’s swimming session start this Saturday?
steps: Find the centre’s current timetable.
Check the date and any closure or change notice.
Record the page title and address so the information can be checked again.
lessons.whyItWorks: Research starts with a question specific enough to investigate. Use search terms that name the topic and the fact you need. Record where each useful claim came from while reading, including title, author or organization, and date when available. This prevents a later list of links from becoming disconnected from the claims they are meant to support.
lessons.watchFor: A search-result snippet can leave out the condition that changes a claim.

lessons.title: Keep source words separate from your explanation
lessons.body: When using a source, preserve its meaning and acknowledge it. A quotation uses the exact words; a paraphrase explains the idea in your own words. Both still need the source. Read the surrounding context.
lessons.example: A report says 8 of 12 respondents used the evening session.
steps: Quote those words exactly if you label them as a quotation.
A fair paraphrase is: Two thirds of the twelve respondents used the evening session.
Name the report and its date; do not change twelve respondents into all residents.
lessons.whyItWorks: Compare sources that bring independent information. Several pages repeating the same original claim are not several independent confirmations. Separate quotation from paraphrase, and preserve the original meaning when paraphrasing. A reference helps another reader trace your work; it does not make a weak or irrelevant source strong.
lessons.watchFor: Do not cite a source you have not actually checked as if you read it.

lessons.title: Compare reasons, not just conclusions
lessons.body: A useful recommendation connects evidence to the decision’s criteria. State what matters: cost, access, time or another need. One option may meet one criterion but fail another. Facts about a different place or date may not fit this decision.
lessons.example: Should a library stay open later?
steps: View A: evening visits suggest a need for access.
View B: staffing records show a higher operating cost.
Both can be true. The decision involves a tradeoff.
lessons.whyItWorks: A viewpoint is shaped by what a person knows, experiences, and values. Identify the actual claim and reasons before agreeing or disagreeing. A reader can understand a viewpoint accurately without accepting every part of it. Look for the strongest fair version of each position rather than selecting a weak sentence that is easy to dismiss.
lessons.watchFor: Describing a position fairly is not the same as endorsing it.

lessons.title: Connect evidence into a position
lessons.body: Compare options against the same criteria. State the trade-off and any important missing fact. If evidence is limited, recommend a small reversible trial or a further check instead of pretending the best choice is certain.
lessons.example: Write a supported recommendation.
steps: Start with a position: trial later opening on one evening.
Give the reason: test demand while limiting extra cost.
State what to measure: additional visits and staffing costs.
lessons.whyItWorks: Compare perspectives using the same question. Identify shared goals, disputed facts, and different priorities separately. Evidence can resolve some factual disputes; a value tradeoff may still require a decision. State where the evidence leads you and what remains uncertain. Fair comparison does not require treating all claims as equally well supported.
lessons.watchFor: Two sides of a disagreement need not have equal amounts or quality of evidence.

lessons.whyItWorks: A project proposal connects a problem with a feasible action. Describe who would benefit, what would be done, who would do it, and which resources are needed. lessons.title: Make the plan reviewable

lessons.whyItWorks: Build a budget and a way to evaluate the result. Separate money already available from money requested. A proposal is an honest plan, not a guarantee.

lessons.title: Describe what you observe without guessing the cause.
lessons.body: An observation records what you see or measure. A guess explains what might have caused it. Keep the record and the guess separate.
lessons.example: There are drops of water on the outside of a cold cup.
steps: Observe the drops and where they are.
Do not immediately conclude the cup leaks.
List a question: where did the outside water come from?
lessons.whyItWorks: An observation tells what you noticed. An explanation tries to say why. Separating them lets another person check the record without accepting your guess first.
lessons.watchFor: A confident explanation is still an inference unless the evidence establishes it.

lessons.title: Record a measurement and test a prediction
lessons.body: A prediction says what you expect before the test; an observation records what happened. Measure with a suitable tool, record its unit, and repeat the test. A ruler reading of 12 cm is a measured length, not a cause.
lessons.example: Work through the reasoning
steps: Choose a suitable tool, such as a ruler.
Read from the same starting point.
Record the value and unit, and note if the reading is approximate.
lessons.whyItWorks: Big means different things to different people. A number and unit are clearer. Add the tool and start and finish points so another person knows how you got the number.
lessons.watchFor: More decimal places do not automatically mean a more accurate measurement.

review: An observation records what you see or measure. A guess explains what might have caused it. Keep the record and the guess separate.

lessons.title: Choose a material using a relevant property.
lessons.body: Choose a material for the job. A cover must keep water out; a towel must absorb it. Transparent means light passes through clearly. A useful property for one job can be unsuitable for another.
lessons.example: Compare a waterproof plastic cover with an absorbent cloth.
steps: For a rain cover, check whether water passes through.
For drying a spill, check how much water the material absorbs.
For seeing through a window, check transparency; one property does not establish every other property.
lessons.whyItWorks: A rain cover and a cleaning cloth need different properties. One should keep water out; the other may need to soak water up. Choose for the purpose, not the name.
lessons.watchFor: A material’s colour alone does not tell you its strength or absorbency.

lessons.title: Test the property you actually need
lessons.body: Compare materials under the same conditions. A material that works for one job may not fit another. Use the test results to explain your choice.

Compare absorbed amounts, rather than choosing the brightest colour.
lessons.whyItWorks: Use the same amount of water, size of sample and time when comparing. Otherwise the difference could come from the test method instead of the material.
lessons.watchFor: One successful trial does not prove a material will work in every condition.

lessons.title: Choose a separation property
lessons.body: A mixture contains materials together. Separate them using a difference in their properties: a sieve sorts by size; a magnet attracts suitable metals; settling can form layers. Sugar dissolved in water is still present even when it is not visible.
lessons.example: A sieve separates particles by size.
steps: Compare the sizes of the two dry materials.
Choose holes that let rice through and retain beans.
Collect both separated materials.
lessons.whyItWorks: Different particle sizes allow a suitable sieve to separate them.
lessons.watchFor: A sieve will not remove dissolved salt.

lessons.title: Check what a filter leaves behind
lessons.body: A filter can trap particles larger than its openings. Dissolved sugar passes through an ordinary particle filter with the water. Evaporating water can leave the sugar behind. Clear water is not evidence that water is safe to drink.
lessons.example: A filter traps suspended sand; dissolved salt passes through.
steps: Place a suitable filter above a collection container.
Pour the mixture through it.
Sand remains in the filter and liquid passes through.
lessons.whyItWorks: A filter blocks particles larger than its pores.
lessons.watchFor: Clear filtered water is not automatically safe to drink.

lessons.title: Compare poles and materials
lessons.body: A magnet attracts some materials, including an ordinary steel paper clip. It does not attract all metals. Its force can act across a small gap. Two north poles repel; a north and a south pole attract.
lessons.example: Steel clips respond; plastic buttons do not.
steps: Bring the magnet near each model object.

lessons.title: Keep a magnet test fair
lessons.body: Magnets have two poles, called north and south. Unlike poles attract. Like poles repel, or push apart. Check the pole labels before predicting the movement.
lessons.example: Unlike poles attract; like poles repel.
steps: Identify each facing pole.
Bring unlike poles close in the model: they attract.
Bring like poles close: they repel.
lessons.whyItWorks: Magnetic poles interact even without touching.

lessons.title: Trace light from a source
lessons.body: Light travels from a source. An object that blocks light makes a shadow behind it. Track the path from the source to the surface.
lessons.example: Lamp → block → shadow on screen
steps: Trace light from the lamp towards the screen.

lessons.title: Explain a changed shadow

lessons.example: Closer to the lamp → a larger shadow on the same screen

Move only the block towards the lamp.

lessons.whyItWorks: The shadow size depends on the geometry of source, object and screen.

units.title: Connect vibrations and sound
units.goal: Explain how vibrations create sound and compare pitch with loudness.
units.why: Explain how vibrations create sound and compare pitch with loudness.

lessons.title: Connect vibration with pitch
lessons.body: Sound comes from vibration and travels through matter such as air or water. Frequency is how often the vibration repeats; higher frequency gives a higher pitch. Sound needs a medium, so it does not travel through a vacuum.
lessons.example: Vibration → surrounding air → sound
steps: The string moves back and forth.
Its movement disturbs the surrounding air.
The changing pressure travels to a listener.
lessons.whyItWorks: Sound is a mechanical vibration travelling through a material.
lessons.watchFor: The source and the travelling sound are not the same object.

lessons.title: Separate pitch and loudness
lessons.body: Amplitude describes the size of a vibration. A larger amplitude usually produces a louder sound under the same conditions; it does not necessarily change pitch. Damping reduces vibration over time. Soft material can absorb some sound energy.
lessons.example: Faster vibration: higher pitch · larger vibration: louder
steps: Compare how often each source vibrates.
Compare the size of the vibrations separately.
Describe pitch and loudness as different properties.
lessons.whyItWorks: Frequency describes repeated cycles; amplitude describes their size.
lessons.watchFor: A high-pitched sound is not automatically loud.

practice.prompt: A tuning fork vibrates faster in the same medium. Which sound feature generally increases?

The colour of the air

practice.explanation: Higher vibration frequency corresponds to higher pitch.

Yes; sound and light always need the same medium.
Only when the label is louder.

practice.explanation: Sound propagates through vibrations in matter.
practice.hint: Compare the choices with the given situation.

practice.prompt: What repeats when a guitar string produces sound?

The creation of new air from nothing

practice.hint: Compare the choices with the given situation.

practice.hint: Compare the choices with the given situation.

lessons.title: Explain how a habitat meets living things’ needs.
lessons.body: A habitat is where a living thing lives. It must provide what that living thing needs. In this simple model, each animal needs one food portion and one shelter.

steps: Plants use light and available resources.

lessons.body: More food may not help if shelter is missing. Food also connects living things: a food chain shows who eats whom. Its arrows follow energy from food to the animal eating it.

units.subject: science
units.title: Predict how a cart changes speed
units.goal: Connect net force, mass and acceleration in a simplified model.
units.why: Connect a change in motion with unbalanced forces.

lessons.title: Connect a change in motion with unbalanced forces.
lessons.body: Velocity includes speed and direction. Balanced forces give zero net force and no change in velocity. In this ideal cart model, acceleration equals net force divided by mass: $a=F/m$. A 6-newton net force on 2 kilograms gives 3 metres per second squared.
lessons.example: A rolling toy car slows down on a rough floor.
steps: Observe the speed decreasing.
Friction and other resistive forces oppose the motion.
The combined force changes the car’s motion.
lessons.whyItWorks: A force is a push or pull with direction. Opposing forces combine into a net force. An object can keep moving with zero net force; a net force changes its motion. In an ideal model, the same force changes the motion of a smaller mass more quickly than a larger mass.
lessons.watchFor: Motion does not by itself prove that the net force is forward.

lessons.title: Distinguish position, speed, and acceleration
lessons.body: Position tells where an object is. Average speed is total distance divided by time. Acceleration describes a change in velocity. With the same net force, more mass gives less acceleration; it does not establish the cart’s current speed. Friction can oppose sliding motion.
lessons.example: A toy car covers 6 metres in 3 seconds
steps: A car covers 6 metres in 3 seconds.
Its average speed is $6\div3=2$ metres per second.
That average does not tell us whether its speed changed during the journey.
lessons.whyItWorks: Average speed uses total distance and total time. It cannot tell whether the car sped up or slowed down along the way. Acceleration needs information about changing velocity. In the cart model, use the combined force and mass: $a=F/m$. Hold one fixed before comparing the other.
lessons.watchFor: Mass and force are different quantities with different units.

units.subject: science
units.title: Make a fair comparison
units.goal: Change one factor and keep a record someone can check.
units.why: Test an idea instead of relying only on a guess.

lessons.title: Change one factor
lessons.body: To test an idea, change the factor you are interested in. Keep other important conditions alike. Decide what to measure before seeing the result.
lessons.example: Does light affect plant growth?
steps: Change: hours of light.
Measure: growth in centimetres over the same time.
Keep similar: plant type, water, soil, and starting size.
lessons.whyItWorks: A fair comparison changes the factor you want to investigate while controlling other important conditions. Decide what you will measure before starting. “Which plant looks nicer?” is less precise than measuring height change over the same number of days. A clear method helps someone else repeat the comparison.
lessons.watchFor: Keeping every condition literally identical is impossible; identify the important controls.

lessons.title: Report what you observed
lessons.body: Record the method and all results, including surprises. Repeating a fair test helps show whether a pattern holds. One result does not prove what always happens.
lessons.example: One group grows 3 cm; the other grows 5 cm.
steps: Observation: one group grew 2 cm more.
Possible conclusion: the light conditions may affect growth.
Next check: repeat with more plants and the same method.
lessons.whyItWorks: If two factors change together, the result may not identify which one mattered. Repeat trials where practical, compare the spread of results, and avoid selecting only the trial that supports your expectation. An unexpected result is information that can help improve the question or method.
lessons.watchFor: A comparison can show an association without proving the proposed cause.

review: A fair comparison changes the factor you want to test while keeping other relevant conditions similar. Record what you change and what you measure before starting.
An observation describes what happened in your test. A conclusion explains what the result suggests. Repetition and more examples help test whether the pattern holds.
Keeping every condition literally identical is impossible; identify the important controls.
A comparison can show an association without proving the proposed cause.

units.title: Track matter through a change
units.goal: Explain a state change without making particles disappear.
units.why: Distinguish a physical change from evidence of a new substance.

lessons.title: Distinguish a physical change from evidence of a new substance.
lessons.body: A solid keeps its shape; a liquid flows but keeps a set volume; a gas spreads through its container. Melting ice changes state without making a new substance: it is a physical change. Rusting makes a new substance: it is chemical.
lessons.example: Ice melts into liquid water.
steps: The state changes from solid to liquid.
The substance is still water.
Cooling can freeze the water again, showing a physical state change.
lessons.whyItWorks: A particle model represents matter as tiny parts. In a change of state, the substance’s particles remain the same kind while their arrangement and motion change. The drawing is a model, not a literal photograph: the spaces, sizes, and colours are chosen to make a relationship understandable.
lessons.watchFor: Particles do not become larger just because a substance expands.

lessons.title: Use evidence without jumping to certainty
lessons.body: Melting changes the state, not which substance it is. A chemical change forms different substances. A colour or temperature change is a clue to investigate, not proof by itself.
lessons.example: Work through the reasoning
steps: Notice bubbles in a warm liquid.

lessons.title: Trace energy transfers without treating energy as used up.
lessons.body: Energy can move between stores or be transferred, rather than being used up. Power is the rate of energy transfer: 1 watt means 1 joule per second. A 10-watt device transfers 30 joules in 3 seconds in this model.
lessons.example: A moving bicycle slows when its brakes are used.
steps: The bicycle’s motion decreases.
Friction transfers energy into thermal stores in the brakes and surroundings.
Energy is transferred, not destroyed by the brakes.
lessons.whyItWorks: Energy accounting follows transfers into, within, and out of a system. Name the system boundary and the useful output. A lamp transfers energy to light and to warming its surroundings; the thermal transfer is still part of the accounting even when it is not the intended purpose. Conservation concerns the total, not just the useful part.
lessons.watchFor: Power and energy are not interchangeable words.

lessons.title: Distinguish energy from power
lessons.body: Double the time at the same power and twice as much energy is transferred. A device can transfer energy usefully and also heat its surroundings. Energy is not simply destroyed.
lessons.example: Work through the reasoning
steps: A device transfers energy at 10 watts.
In 3 seconds, $E=10\times3=30$ joules.
Doubling the time at that power doubles the energy transferred.
lessons.whyItWorks: Power describes how quickly energy is transferred. The same device used twice as long at constant power transfers twice as much energy. A high-power device can transfer less total energy than a lower-power device if it runs for much less time. Compare both power and duration before deciding which used more energy.
lessons.watchFor: Energy described as wasted has been transferred; it has not disappeared.

lessons.title: Connect cell parts to their jobs
lessons.body: Cells have structures with jobs. The membrane controls entry and exit; the nucleus contains genetic information; ribosomes make proteins; mitochondria support energy-releasing processes. Plant cells also have a cell wall, and many have chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
lessons.example: A simplified animal cell
steps: Find the membrane: it controls exchange with the surroundings.
Find the ribosomes: they build proteins the cell needs.
Find the mitochondria: they help transfer energy into a form the cell can use.
lessons.whyItWorks: A cell model links structures with functions. A boundary controls exchanges, internal structures carry out processes, and genetic information helps direct activity. Different cells can have different structures and roles. A diagram simplifies their shapes and relative sizes; focus first on which function each label represents.
lessons.watchFor: Not every cell has every structure shown in one textbook diagram.

lessons.title: Connect cells into a bigger system
lessons.body: Cells can work together in tissues, organs and systems. A diagram leaves out much of their detail. This model shows a typical animal cell; it does not describe every kind of cell.
lessons.example: Muscle cells help an arm move
steps: Muscle cells can contract. They work together in muscle tissue.
Muscles work with bones, nerves and other parts so the arm can move.
A flat cell diagram helps name parts. It cannot show every shape, size or interaction.
lessons.whyItWorks: A multicellular organism depends on coordinated parts. Cells form tissues, tissues contribute to organs, and organs work within systems. A change in one part can affect others because materials and information move between them. Avoid treating a single diagram as a complete account of every cell or every organism.
lessons.watchFor: A label names a structure; understanding also requires saying what it does.

lessons.title: Read data with units, variation, and uncertainty.
lessons.body: Read axis labels, units and scale before comparing points. A higher plotted value is not necessarily a larger physical amount if the units differ. Association means values vary together; it alone does not prove that one causes the other.
lessons.example: Ice cream sales and swimming visits both rise in warm weather.
steps: Notice the association.
Temperature could influence both quantities.
Do not conclude that buying ice cream causes people to swim.
lessons.whyItWorks: Read the axes, units, sample, and method before interpreting a graph. Separate the measured pattern from a proposed explanation. A rising line describes a relationship in the displayed data; it does not automatically identify a cause. Check whether a different scale makes the same change appear more dramatic.
lessons.watchFor: A graph can be accurately drawn yet support a narrower claim than its headline.

lessons.title: Check the strength of a conclusion
lessons.body: Interpolation estimates between measured points; extrapolation estimates beyond them and needs more caution. Repeated measurements show variation. Investigate an unusual result rather than silently deleting it. A model should not claim more precision than its data support.
lessons.example: Work through the reasoning
steps: Read the measured range before predicting.
Check whether a trend is consistent and repeated.
Label predictions beyond that range as less secure.
lessons.whyItWorks: Look for repeated patterns, variation, and exceptions. An unusual point may be an error, an important event, or ordinary variation; investigate rather than deleting it automatically. The size and selection of a sample affect how widely you can generalize. A useful conclusion states both the result and its limits.
lessons.watchFor: Correlation alone does not identify the direction or cause of a relationship.

review: Read axis labels, units and scale before comparing points. A higher plotted value is not necessarily a larger physical amount if the units differ. Association means values vary together; it alone does not prove that one causes the other.

lessons.title: Describe reactions using particles and conservation.
lessons.body: A chemical formula names atoms and their counts. In H2O, each water molecule has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. A coefficient counts molecules: 3 H2O means 3 water molecules, containing 6 hydrogen atoms and 3 oxygen atoms.
lessons.example: $2H_2+O_2\rightarrow2H_2O$
steps: Left: four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms.
Right: two water molecules contain four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms.
The counts match; the atoms have been rearranged.
lessons.whyItWorks: Chemical equations account for atoms. In a reaction, bonds can change and atoms are rearranged into different groupings. In a closed system, the number of each kind of atom is conserved. Count each type on both sides of a model before deciding whether the equation represents a possible rearrangement.
lessons.watchFor: A gas leaving an open container can make the measured container mass fall without destroying atoms.

lessons.title: Count whole molecules and track escaping matter
lessons.body: A reaction rearranges atoms into new substances. Balance the number of each kind of atom using coefficients; changing a formula changes the substance. In a closed system, matter cannot enter or leave, so total mass is conserved.
lessons.example: Read the count, then check the boundary
steps: In $2H_2$, the coefficient 2 counts two molecules. Each contains two hydrogen atoms: $2\times2=4$ atoms.
Changing $H_2$ to $H_3$ would change the formula. It would not be a valid way to balance this equation.
If a reaction releases gas from an open cup, count the escaped gas as well as what remains. The cup can get lighter without atoms being destroyed.
lessons.whyItWorks: Coefficients change the number of complete molecules; subscripts change what a molecule is. To balance an equation, adjust whole-molecule counts rather than quietly changing the substance. Our coloured-particle example is a bookkeeping model, not instructions for mixing real chemicals. Use it to track what stays constant during a change.
lessons.watchFor: Do not change a formula’s subscript to make an equation appear balanced.

lessons.title: Use voltage and resistance
lessons.body: Current is the flow of electric charge, measured in amperes. Voltage describes energy transferred per unit of charge. Resistance, in ohms, relates voltage and current. For an ohmic resistor, $V=IR$: 8 volts across 4 ohms gives 2 amperes.
lessons.example: 9 volts across an ideal 3-ohm resistor
steps: Identify voltage $V=9\ \mathrm{V}$ and resistance $R=3\ \Omega$.
Divide: $I=V/R=9/3=3\ \mathrm{A}$.
Keep voltage at 9 V and double resistance to 6 ohms. Current halves: $I=9/6=1.5\ \mathrm{A}$.
lessons.whyItWorks: Current is the rate of charge flow, while potential difference describes energy transferred per unit charge. In a simple resistor model, increasing voltage at fixed resistance increases current. Increasing resistance at fixed voltage reduces current. This relationship is useful for an idealized resistor; not every electrical device behaves as a constant resistor.
lessons.watchFor: Current does not mean the amount of energy stored in a battery.

lessons.title: Count cycles and compare height
lessons.body: Frequency counts cycles per second, in hertz. Period is the time for one cycle; frequency equals 1 divided by period. Amplitude is the size from the middle to a peak; it can change without changing frequency. Wavelength measures one complete spatial cycle. In one medium, $v=f\lambda$.
lessons.example: A wave repeats every half second
steps: The period is the time for one complete cycle: $T=0.5\ \mathrm{s}$.
Frequency counts cycles per second: $f=1/T=1/0.5=2\ \mathrm{Hz}$.
Doubling the height from the middle to a peak changes amplitude. If each cycle still takes half a second, frequency stays 2 Hz.
lessons.whyItWorks: A wave’s amplitude and frequency describe different features. Amplitude measures the size of its variation; frequency counts cycles per second. Changing frequency packs more cycles into the same time interval without necessarily making the wave taller. Read the time axis before deciding whether a wave has a higher frequency.
lessons.watchFor: A taller wave is not automatically a faster oscillation.

lessons.title: Use a model and state where it may fail.
lessons.body: A model keeps some features and leaves others out. It can help you predict, but only under its assumptions. Compare its answer with what the situation could actually allow.
lessons.example: A constant-speed model predicts distance using $d=vt$.
steps: Assumption: speed stays constant over the interval.
At 2 metres per second for 5 seconds, $d=10$ metres.
A stop or acceleration breaks that assumption, so the prediction needs adjustment.
lessons.whyItWorks: A scientific model represents selected relationships to answer a question. Identify what it includes, what it leaves out, and where it has been compared with evidence. A straight-line model may work over a short interval while missing limits that appear later. A model’s usefulness depends on its purpose and range.
lessons.watchFor: A model is not a complete copy of reality.

lessons.title: Compare predictions with observations
lessons.body: A tank starts empty, holds 20 litres and receives 2 litres per minute. The rule $V=2t$ predicts volume before the tank is full. At 10 minutes it reaches capacity; after that, the rule needs an overflow model.
lessons.example: Check the empty 20-litre tank at 8, 10 and 12 minutes.
steps: At 8 minutes, $2(8)=16$ litres fits the tank.
At 10 minutes, $2(10)=20$ litres fills it.
At 12 minutes the same rule predicts 24 litres, exceeding capacity. Separate water delivered from water held in the tank.
lessons.whyItWorks: Compare predictions with observations and inspect the differences. If the model misses systematically, revise its assumptions or restrict its use. A good fit to existing points does not prove every future prediction. Testing a new situation is more informative than repeatedly checking the same example used to build the model.
lessons.watchFor: A precise numerical prediction can still rely on an unrealistic assumption.

units.goal: Open your tools, move between them, and make the screen comfortable.
units.why: You do not have to remember every button. Learn a few ways to find your place and return to your work.

lessons.title: An app does a job. A file keeps your work.
lessons.body: Open the tool you need. Move between its window and another app. Adjust the screen so you can see the task and its controls.
lessons.whyItWorks: These are different layers. A notes app can open several note files. A browser can show several tabs. The taskbar helps you return to an open app; Start helps you find one. Scroll to see more of a page. Single-click selects many items; double-click opens many files. A right-click, or touch-and-hold, often opens an item menu. Moving or resizing a window changes your view, not the saved file.
lessons.example: Keep a shopping note open while checking a calendar.
steps: Open Start and choose Notes in this practice screen.
Open Calendar too. Use its taskbar button to switch, then return to Notes.
Make Notes smaller so you can see both tools. Its saved note stays the same.
lessons.watchFor: Minimise hides a window. Close ends that window. Neither is the same as deleting a saved file.

lessons.title: Set the computer up for you
lessons.body: Try one setting at a time. Check whether it helps you use the tool. Undo a change that makes the task harder.
lessons.whyItWorks: Comfort settings help you spend attention on the task. There is no best text size for everyone. Lock protects an open session. Sleep saves power for a break; restart closes and reloads the system; shutdown turns it off. Save first because unsaved work may be lost when apps close.
lessons.example: Ari cannot read a small note and needs a short break.
steps: Open Settings, then Accessibility. Try larger text and check the preview.
Apply a size that fits. Keyboard, captions, pointer and volume settings can also help.
Save the note. Lock the screen for the break. Sign in privately when returning.

lessons.whyItWorks: The cursor is the small mark showing where your next character goes. A gap is a character too. If you type two spaces, the words may look farther apart. lessons.whyItWorks: A familiar starting place can make keys easier to find. You can try resting your left fingers near A S D F and right fingers near J K L ;, then reach for a key and come back. This is a suggestion, not a required body position. One-hand input, larger keys, speech or another layout can also produce useful writing. Short relaxed practice is more useful than forcing a painful session.

lessons.whyItWorks: The cursor position and selection decide what changes. First look for the highlight. Ctrl+A selects all on Windows; Ctrl+C copies and Ctrl+V pastes. Ctrl+Z usually undoes. units.why: A calm plan keeps a small sign-in problem from turning into a lost account or a scam.

lessons.title: Recovery is a plan, not a shared password
lessons.body: A password lets you sign in. A recovery method helps when sign-in fails. Keep both private. Start recovery from the service you know, not an unexpected message.
lessons.whyItWorks: Someone offering help does not need to know every secret. A mentor can sit beside you while you follow official steps privately. A second sign-in factor adds another check; recovery codes can also unlock access and need protection. A plan names a trusted route and safe storage, without writing the secrets into schoolwork.
lessons.example: Jo receives a message asking for a sign-in code.
steps: Do not reply with the code. Stop using the message link.

If locked out, use its official recovery route. Keep private details off the shared screen.
lessons.watchFor: A familiar logo, friendly name or urgent tone does not prove who is asking.

lessons.title: Updates come through a route you can check
lessons.body: A browser advert saying you have viruses is not your system update screen. Open Settings yourself. Read the status. Save work and plan a restart if needed.
lessons.whyItWorks: A message can imitate a trusted brand. Opening the real settings independently avoids trusting its link or phone number. Updates change software and may need time or power. A failed update calls for its actual error and official help, not a random cleaner. A successful simulation does not prove the computer is supported or updated.

steps: Leave the warning alone. Do not call its number or install its tool.

Read the real status and choose a supported next step. Ask for help when it is unclear.
lessons.watchFor: Never disable protection just to satisfy an installer, an advert or an unexplained AI instruction.

lessons.title: Plan a work task with time to check it.
lessons.body: A plan connects a goal to the jobs, time and resources it needs. Some jobs depend on earlier steps. Name the dependency so a delay does not stay hidden.
lessons.example: Prepare ten information packs before 2 pm.
steps: Check the required contents and materials.
Arrange the steps: print, assemble, then check.
Allow time for missing pages or a printing delay.
lessons.whyItWorks: A work plan connects the outcome to actions, resources, and time. Identify which steps depend on earlier ones and which can happen independently. Estimate with some room for ordinary delays. A checklist carries information outside your memory, leaving more attention for the task itself.
lessons.watchFor: A list of tasks is not yet a schedule unless it accounts for order and time.

lessons.title: Update a plan when conditions change
lessons.body: When a resource is unavailable, update the estimate. Offer a workable option and ask the responsible person to confirm the priority. An estimate is not a guarantee.
lessons.example: Work through the reasoning
steps: Identify which step is delayed.
Estimate the effect on the finish time.
Ask whether to change scope, get help, or move the deadline.
lessons.whyItWorks: Update the plan when a condition changes. State the effect on the deadline and offer realistic choices, such as reducing scope or asking for another person’s help. Confirm the revised priority with the person who can decide. Reporting a delay early gives more options than hiding it until the end.
lessons.watchFor: Promising an impossible deadline does not resolve conflicting priorities.

units.goal: Use a job posting to write an honest application that fits your time and skills.
units.why: You can explain what you bring even if this would be your first paid job.

lessons.title: Turn the posting into a short plan
lessons.body: A posting is a notice for a job. A resume is a short account of your skills and experience. Find the tasks, hours, place and how to apply. Then compare them with what you can actually do.
lessons.whyItWorks: A useful example says what you did and what happened. Paid work is not the only source of an example: helping at an event can show careful counting or following instructions. Keep it true. Availability means the times you can work, including travel. Do not promise a start time you cannot reach.
lessons.example: Fictional Corner Shop needs a shelf helper, Saturday 10 am to 2 pm. Apply with a short message and resume through its verified website. Ari counted supplies at a community event and can reach the shop by 9:45 am.
steps: Match the task: counting event supplies is relevant to checking shelf stock. Describe the action without claiming a job Ari never held.
From 10 am to noon is two hours; noon to 2 pm adds two more. The span is $2+2=4$ hours. Arrival at 9:45 am leaves 15 minutes before the start.
Draft a message naming the role, the useful example and the available time. Follow the posting’s instructions for the resume.
lessons.watchFor: Saying “I can do everything” gives less evidence than one clear, truthful example.

lessons.title: A changed detail needs a changed reply
lessons.body: Before sending, check the role, time and contact. A reference is someone who can describe your work; ask them first. Keep your Social Insurance Number (SIN) and banking details out of a resume. Check unexpected requests through a separate known contact.
lessons.whyItWorks: A message can look official and still be fake. A company name or friendly tone is not enough to verify it. Job Bank warns about job requests for money or sensitive information. Hiring and payroll are later steps with a verified employer. You can ask a question, suggest a workable time or decline a mismatch.
lessons.example: New detail: the shop asks about Friday 3 pm to 7 pm instead. Ari finishes class at 3:30 pm and needs 30 minutes to travel. A separate text asks for a deposit to hold the job.
steps: Ari could reach the shop at 4 pm. That misses the requested start by 60 minutes.
Revise the message: explain the actual available time and ask whether a 4 pm start or Saturday shift is possible. Do not claim the change is agreed.
Pause the deposit request. Check with the shop using its independently verified contact, without paying through the text.
lessons.watchFor: An application is a request to be considered. It is not a job offer or a guarantee of work.

units.subject: work
units.title: Get ready for your first shift
units.goal: Plan a shift, check the instructions and ask for the training or support needed.
units.why: Knowing where to go, what to ask and when to stop guessing makes a first day easier.

lessons.title: Make the day concrete
lessons.body: Write down the day, start time, place and person to meet. Ask about the finish time, breaks and pay. CAD means Canadian dollars. Plan the trip both ways. Leave enough time to find the entrance.
lessons.whyItWorks: A time span and paid hours are different things. A stated unpaid break must be subtracted from the span. Manitoba generally requires a 30-minute break after five consecutive hours; responsibility-free breaks are usually unpaid. Check the actual arrangement. Keep your own hours record. Travel planning is not an instruction to perform unpaid work.
lessons.example: Fictional schedule: 9 am to 3 pm, with a stated unpaid 30-minute break from noon to 12:30 pm. Travel takes 35 minutes; Jo wants 10 extra minutes to find the entrance.
steps: Allow $35+10=45$ minutes for travel and finding the place. Leave at 8:15 am for a 9 am start.
The span is six hours. The stated break is half an hour: $6-0.5=5.5$ paid hours.
At the fictional rate of 20 CAD per hour, base pay is $5.5\times20=110$ CAD before deductions. Other pay rules may also apply.
lessons.watchFor: Do not subtract a “break” while doing tasks. Ask about that situation instead.

lessons.title: Ask, confirm, then do the task
lessons.body: You can ask for a demonstration or written steps. Repeat the plan in your own words and check it. If an instruction is unclear or unsafe, stop guessing and tell the person in charge.
lessons.whyItWorks: For an ordinary Manitoba retail job at ages 13–15, check the approved Young Worker Readiness Certificate Course, parent or guardian signature, direct adult supervision, task limits and permitted hours. The school-week limit is 20 hours, with no work from 11 pm to 6 am. Different rules or exceptions may apply to other work. A support request should explain what helps; it does not need private medical details in this app.
lessons.example: Fictional change: Jo is 15 and already has 18 work hours scheduled in a school week. The shop proposes three more. Jo also wants written steps for the stock task.
steps: The proposed total is $18+3=21$ hours. That is one hour above the stated 20-hour school-week limit. Jo needs a revised plan, not an automatic yes.
Jo asks the supervisor to check the hours and required youth arrangements. If a required signature is unavailable, Jo can ask Employment Standards about the situation.
Jo asks for the stock steps in writing and a demonstration, then confirms who will check the first attempt. Stepstone cannot issue the required certificate.
lessons.watchFor: Being confident or having a high quiz score does not replace training, supervision or required permission.

practice.prompt: A trip takes 30 minutes and the plan adds 15 minutes for finding the entrance. How many minutes should be allowed?
practice.explanation: $30+15=45$ minutes before the start.
practice.hint: Use the numbers in this made-up case. Label what you are counting.

Being confident or having a high quiz score does not replace training, supervision or required permission.
State what you know, what you need to check, and who can help.

steps: Confirm the date, place, contact person, hours, rate, break plan and tasks. Check the trip there and back. Record hours worked, including required work activities.

For a real job, check the current Manitoba young-worker rules and required course for your age and work. Ask Employment Standards if the required parent or guardian is unavailable; do not invent consent or assume an app mentor can sign instead.

Ask who will train you and how to report a problem. Explain any instruction or access needs. Confirm the arrangement. For dangerous work, use the official reporting and refusal process; app messages are not urgent safety monitoring.

units.subject: work
units.title: Explain a real job example
units.goal: Use a real example
units.why: Talk about what you can do and learn about a job.

lessons.title: Use a real example
lessons.body: A useful job example can come from a project, volunteering or daily life. Describe the situation, what you did and what happened. Do not invent experience.
lessons.example: Tell me about a strength.
steps: Name the skill: I keep things organised.
Give an example: I labelled and sorted our shared tools.
Say the result: People could find what they needed.
lessons.whyItWorks: A job conversation is a chance to connect your experience with the task. Use a specific example: describe the situation, what you did, and what happened or what you learned. Examples can come from projects, volunteering, study, or responsibilities outside paid work. Do not invent experience to make the answer sound stronger.
lessons.watchFor: Eye contact and fast answers are not the same as understanding or competence.

lessons.title: Explain what you learned
lessons.body: A follow-up may ask for a detail or what you would change. Answer that question using the same real example. Separate what happened from what you would do next time. Ask for clarification when the follow-up is unclear.
lessons.example: Your first set of labels missed a date. The next set included it.
steps: State the issue: my first labels missed the date.
Explain your correction: I checked a sample with the organiser and added the date.
Name the lesson: next time I would confirm a sample before making the whole set.
lessons.whyItWorks: You can ask for a question to be repeated or for a moment to think. You can also ask what the role involves and how instructions are provided. The aim is an accurate exchange about the work, not a performance of a particular personality. Practice a short answer and revise the parts that feel unclear.
lessons.watchFor: A memorized script needs adapting when the actual question changes.

review: A useful job example can come from a project, volunteering or daily life. Describe the situation, what you did and what happened. Do not invent experience.

A follow-up may ask for a detail or what you would change. Answer that question using the same real example. Separate what happened from what you would do next time. Ask for clarification when the follow-up is unclear.
units.reflection: The interviewer asks what you would change next time. Add a specific lesson from your invented practice example; do not invent real work history. Explain one choice in your reply.

practice.hint: Compare the choices with the given situation.

practice.hint: Compare the choices with the given situation.

practice.hint: Compare the choices with the given situation.

units.subject: work
units.title: Handle a work or pay problem
units.goal: Check a pay record, describe the problem and choose the right kind of help.
units.why: A clear record and a specific question make it easier to act when something is wrong.

lessons.title: Compare the same dates and labels
lessons.body: CAD means Canadian dollars. A pay period is the set of dates covered by a payment. Gross pay is before deductions; net pay is after them. Match your hours record with that period before comparing the numbers.
lessons.whyItWorks: Multiplying hours by a rate checks basic pay for those hours. A full statement can also include overtime, vacation pay and other items. Manitoba’s guidance explains pay statements and record keeping. A difference is a reason to check the labels and ask a precise question, not proof by itself of what happened.
lessons.example: Fictional records: Ren lists 18 regular hours at CAD 20 per hour. The statement lists 16 hours and CAD 320 base pay. The pay-period dates still need checking.
steps: For 18 hours, the base calculation is $18\times20=360$ CAD.
The difference from the listed base pay is $360-320=40$ CAD. This compares base amounts, not the bank deposit.
Ask which dates the 16 hours cover. Mention the two records and request an explanation or correction. Keep a copy of the reply.
lessons.watchFor: A bank deposit is usually a net amount. Comparing it directly with basic gross pay can create a false alarm.

lessons.title: Update the facts and choose who can help
lessons.body: A new fact can change the problem. Correct your calculation if needed, then name the issue that remains. Pay, dangerous work and disability-related support have different help routes. You do not need to solve them alone.
lessons.whyItWorks: Manitoba’s deductions guidance lists cash shortages among costs an employer cannot take from wages. Employment Standards can explain wage concerns and claim routes. Workplace Safety and Health handles unsafe-work concerns. Disability-related adjustments concern access to doing the job; Manitoba’s human rights guidance explains that process. A practice answer cannot decide an individual case.
lessons.example: New facts: two of Ren’s 18 hours were after this pay period ended, so 16 belong here. But the same statement also shows CAD 40 taken for a cash shortage.
steps: Revise the base comparison: $16\times20=320$ CAD. The base-hours difference for this period is zero; check the later two hours on the next statement.
The separate cash-shortage deduction still needs attention. Ask for it to be checked against Manitoba’s deduction rules, and seek Employment Standards help if needed.
For a separate dangerous-machine concern, report to the person in charge and use the safety process. Do not send only a pay query and wait for it to solve a safety issue.
lessons.watchFor: Checking with the employer is not a requirement to wait indefinitely or give up access to official help.

practice.prompt: Use this fictional basic calculation: 12 regular hours at CAD 20 per hour. What is the base pay before other items, in CAD?
practice.explanation: $12\times20=240$ CAD.
practice.hint: Use the numbers in this made-up case. Label what you are counting.

practice.explanation: Gross and net measure different stages of the pay calculation.

options.text: Move those hours to the next-period check and recalculate this period.
Keep claiming they belong to both periods.

practice.explanation: Revise the calculation when the evidence changes.
practice.hint: Name the goal, the evidence you have, and the detail that still needs checking.

options.text: Manitoba Employment Standards.
The driver licensing office.

practice.explanation: Use the wage-help route and check any claim time limit.
practice.hint: Name the goal, the evidence you have, and the detail that still needs checking.

options.text: Manitoba’s human rights and reasonable-accommodation guidance.

practice.explanation: Accommodation means changing how something is done to address an individual protected need; check the process and situation.
practice.hint: Name the goal, the evidence you have, and the detail that still needs checking.

review: A bank deposit is usually a net amount. Comparing it directly with basic gross pay can create a false alarm.
Checking with the employer is not a requirement to wait indefinitely or give up access to official help.
State what you know, what you need to check, and who can help.
units.reflection: Using Ren’s fictional case, explain what the new dates changed, what issue remains and which help route fits it.

steps: Keep hours, pay statements and relevant messages privately. Match the pay-period dates, rate, hours and deductions before comparing totals. Ask about unclear amounts.

For a pay question, ask payroll or the employer to explain or correct the specific item. Contact Employment Standards for help. Its claims page says to file within six months of the last day of work or of the incident, so check the dates promptly. It also directs federally regulated work to a different office. If represented by a union, ask your representative about the relevant process.

For dangerous conditions, tell the person in charge and follow the official refusal/reporting process; contact Workplace Safety and Health if unresolved. For disability-related adjustments or discrimination, use Manitoba’s human rights guidance. Immediate danger needs real-world help, not an app reply.

units.goal: Give and use feedback about a specific action.
units.why: Give and use feedback about a specific action.

lessons.title: Give and use feedback about a specific action.
lessons.body: Useful feedback names an action and its effect. It can show what to keep and what to change. A comment about one piece of work is not a verdict about you.
lessons.example: A teammate’s labels are clear, but one date is missing.
steps: Recognise the useful feature: the labels are easy to read.
Identify the specific issue: one label lacks a date.
Ask for the date to be added and checked.
lessons.whyItWorks: Useful feedback identifies an observable action, its effect, and a possible next step. “The date is missing, so I cannot schedule it” gives more guidance than “this is bad.” Ask what the receiver wants feedback on, and distinguish a requirement from your personal preference.
lessons.watchFor: Praise without a specific observation may not tell someone what to repeat.

lessons.title: Turn feedback into a next attempt
lessons.body: Ask for an example if feedback is vague. Compare it with the task requirements. Make a useful change, or show why a correction may be based on the wrong version.
lessons.example: Work through the reasoning
steps: Ask which part needs changing.
Compare the feedback with the task’s requirements.
Make a relevant revision or explain the evidence for a different view.
lessons.whyItWorks: When receiving feedback, check the specific change being requested. You can ask for an example or explain a relevant constraint. Decide what to try, then compare the result. lessons.title: Link the change to the task
lessons.body: Name the job and what gets in the way. Ask for a change that helps with that problem. You can start with a short sentence: Could I have the steps in writing?
lessons.whyItWorks: A specific request connects the barrier to the task: fast spoken instructions are hard to follow, so written steps may help. An adjustment changes how a person can take part; it does not automatically remove the task’s safety needs. Manitoba’s accommodation guidance describes changes for needs protected by human-rights law. Individual decisions depend on the situation.

steps: Name the task: pack the order accurately and safely.

lessons.watchFor: A specific request starts a discussion. It does not guarantee that one exact option will be approved.

lessons.title: Try, review and protect private details
lessons.body: Check whether the change helps with the job. Say what works and what still gets in the way. Ask how any needed private information should be handled. Keep it out of this lesson.
lessons.whyItWorks: An adjustment can partly help. Compare the result with the goal, then refine the plan. A formal work accommodation request may need relevant supporting information; that is different from handing over a complete medical file. Ask what is needed, why, and who will see it. Human-rights guidance and a responsible person can help with the real process.

lessons.whyItWorks: Define the workplace problem in terms of a result that is not being achieved. Gather relevant facts, identify who can decide, and compare more than one possible response. lessons.title: Choose and evaluate an option

lessons.whyItWorks: A solution needs follow-through. Name the person responsible, the next action, and a way to check whether it helped. If the evidence shows it did not work, revise the approach. Document a useful handoff so the next person does not have to reconstruct the whole situation from scattered messages.

units.title: Make a plan you can actually use
units.goal: Make a realistic plan for time, money, and asking for help.
units.why: Handle appointments, costs, and changes one manageable step at a time.

lessons.title: Work backward from the actual task
lessons.body: Work backwards from an appointment time. Include travel, waiting and preparation. Use money you actually have. List what to bring and which details need confirming.
lessons.whyItWorks: The plan should fit the resources you actually have. Separate a required cost from an optional choice, but remember that needs vary by person. Use invented numbers here; the app does not need your real bank information or home situation. The practical money modules provide more calculation practice.
lessons.example: An invented appointment starts at 2 pm
steps: Allow 30 minutes for travel and 10 minutes of buffer.
Be ready to leave at 1:20 pm.
Confirm the place and what to bring before that day.
lessons.watchFor: An optimistic travel estimate without any buffer can make the rest of a plan fragile.

lessons.title: Revise instead of giving up
lessons.body: A delay or extra cost changes the plan. Update the numbers and choose a workable backup. Ask for help early when the plan no longer fits; do not hide the missing time or money.
lessons.whyItWorks: A short checklist can make a big task easier to start. Choose one action that can be done now, then the next. For a job application, gather truthful examples, check the role, write a clear message, and review the final file. Ask for specific help where it is useful. You do not have to pretend every part is easy.
lessons.example: A practice budget has 60 dollars available
steps: Travel costs 12 dollars and materials cost 30, leaving $60-12-30=18$.
An optional 25-dollar item does not fit: it exceeds the remainder by 7 dollars.
Revise the optional choice or timing; do not invent extra available money.
lessons.watchFor: A planned reward that is not funded is not money you already have.

lessons.title: Install for a job, not for a collection
lessons.body: Name the job first. Try a tool already installed. If you need another, check the real publisher and download route. Read the installer. Cancel any unexpected extra.
lessons.whyItWorks: An app needs a reason to be on the computer. A document editor helps write and open files; a code editor can wait until a project needs it. Search adverts, familiar icons and filenames can imitate a real publisher. Check the source independently and understand requests for access before accepting them.

lessons.title: Keep, remove, or ask first
lessons.body: Keep tools you need. Remove a known unwanted app through normal settings. Ask before touching something unfamiliar. Drivers help hardware work; protection and access tools have important jobs.
lessons.whyItWorks: Bloat is not a precise technical category. A preinstalled trial may be optional while a plain-looking driver is essential. A reversible, one-at-a-time choice lets you check what changed. Blanket removal scripts hide many decisions in one click. Record the reason and do not remove an app merely because you dislike its name.

lessons.title: Keep a checked, separate backup
lessons.body: A backup is an extra copy you can recover. Save important work to an agreed separate location. Open the copy and check the latest change before relying on it.
lessons.whyItWorks: Separate storage can keep work available after the original device fails. Opening the copy checks that it contains usable work.

lessons.whyItWorks: A useful report separates observation from a guess. “The file is not in the folder I checked” is more precise than “the computer deleted everything.” A helper can then test a small next step. lessons.title: Give your app one useful job
lessons.body: An app takes something in, follows a rule, and shows a result. Start with a job you understand. A checklist can remember what to pack. An inventory can count supplies. A planner can add practice minutes. A saving tracker can compare saved amounts with a goal.
lessons.whyItWorks: The input is what you enter. The rule decides what is allowed and what to do. The output is what changes on screen. For a checklist: type “water”, reject an empty name, then show a new item. A condition is an if decision. A limit is also a rule: if six items already exist, do not add a seventh. A label tells someone what to enter; it is not the stored value. Changing the label should not erase the list.
lessons.example: Sketch a shift checklist
steps: Write the job: help me remember what to take. Leave payments and public sharing out of this first version.
Name three behaviours: add an item, mark it done, keep it after I return. Sketch a title, input box, button and list.
Predict: with two items, adding one makes $2+1=3$. An empty name should leave the count at $2$.
lessons.watchFor: A plan and a working app are different. In Your useful app, build the version and add a real practice item before calling it working.

lessons.title: Make one change. Check it. Keep a way back.
lessons.body: Before a change, save a working copy. Say what should happen. Change one small part, then compare the result with your prediction. Try ordinary input, empty input, the edge of a limit, and an invalid value. A nice-looking screen can still have a wrong calculation.
lessons.whyItWorks: A boundary is the edge of an allowed range. If the maximum is six items, test six and then a seventh. Invalid means the input breaks a rule, such as a word in a quantity box. When a check fails, first compare the observed result with the stated rule. Undo can return to a recent version; a separate backup helps after browser data is cleared. The app HTML and the data backup do different jobs: HTML is the tool, the backup is its saved contents.
lessons.example: Check a small saving tracker
steps: Predict that “ten” is rejected. If a label change also breaks the total, undo it and inspect the smaller change.
Download the app and a data backup. Reopen the app, restore the backup and compare the items and total. Try keyboard controls and a phone or narrow window; describe which you actually used.
lessons.watchFor: A paid AI plan is optional. If asking AI, name one change, the existing behaviour to keep, and a test. Read code changes before running them; never add passwords, payment access or unexplained commands.

units.goal: Scale a simple meal, shop for what is missing and make a workable backup.
units.why: Food planning combines counting, reading and choices. Start with the food, time and equipment available.

lessons.title: Make the right amount for the people
lessons.body: A recipe states how many portions it makes. To make twice as many, double each ingredient. Check what you already have, then list what is missing.
lessons.whyItWorks: The same scale factor keeps the ingredient amounts in the same proportion. It does not automatically double cooking time. This cold-wrap example uses ready-to-eat ingredients and clean hands and utensils. Real portions and food choices depend on the people; this model is for practising a method.
lessons.example: Practice recipe: two lunch packs use two wraps, 250 mL beans and 250 mL vegetables. Each wrap is cut into two halves.
steps: For four packs, $4\div2=2$: multiply each ingredient amount by two. Use four wraps, 500 mL beans and 500 mL vegetables.
There is one wrap, 250 mL beans and 250 mL vegetables already available. The missing amounts are three wraps, 250 mL beans and 250 mL vegetables.
The fictional shop sells four wraps together. Buying that pack plus the missing beans and vegetables costs $4+3+4=11$ dollars. CAD 12 leaves CAD 1; one bought wrap is spare.
lessons.watchFor: The amount needed and the package you must buy can differ. Check the package price and what you will do with any extra.

lessons.title: More people means a new plan
lessons.body: If more people join, recount the portions and costs. Check that a cheaper ingredient fits the meal and people. Plan safe storage as well as preparation.
lessons.whyItWorks: Six packs need three times the two-pack recipe: six wraps and 750 mL each of beans and vegetables. With the same pantry amounts, five wraps and 500 mL of each filling are missing. Compare whole purchase costs, not just the cheapest sticker. Store leftovers promptly; cooked food left at room temperature over two hours should be discarded, not judged by smell.
lessons.example: For 6 packs, buy a 6-wrap pack for 6 dollars, 500 mL beans for 4 dollars and 500 mL vegetables for 4 dollars. Pantry stock is 1 wrap and 250 mL each of beans and vegetables; the limit is 12 dollars.
steps: Six packs need 6 wraps and 750 mL each of beans and vegetables. Subtract the stated pantry stock: 5 wraps and 500 mL of each are missing.
The new shopping options cost 6 + 4 + 4 = 14 dollars. The 6-wrap pack leaves one wrap spare with the pantry wrap.
A listed 500 mL vegetable option costs 2 dollars instead of 4. Using it makes the complete purchase 12 dollars, meeting the limit.
lessons.watchFor: Do not scale cooking temperature or cooking time just because portions increase. Do not stretch a budget by relying on food whose storage was unsafe.

steps: Choose meals and snacks that fit the people, available time, equipment and storage. Check food already on hand, labels and allergies or other food needs. Use a suitable recipe rather than guessing cooking instructions.

Follow current food-safety instructions for preparation and storage. If money or access is the obstacle, Harvest Manitoba can explain food-support options. Asking for food support is a practical step, not a failed lesson.

lessons.title: Follow the cooking steps
lessons.body: Read the recipe and the correct food category in the cooking-temperature chart. Check the internal temperature with a clean digital food thermometer; colour alone is not a reliable test. Attend to the cooking and use the stated target for that food.

steps: Read the recipe and prepare the cooking equipment.

lessons.title: Put leftovers away
lessons.body: Divide cooked leftovers into clean shallow containers and refrigerate promptly. Discard cooked food left at room temperature for more than two hours. Label contents and date; plan to use refrigerated leftovers within 2 to 3 days or freeze them.

lessons.title: Reheat a portion
lessons.body: Reheat properly stored leftovers to an internal temperature of 74°C. Use a suitable container, follow its venting instructions and stir during microwave reheating. Check with a clean thermometer. A normal smell cannot establish safety or undo unsuitable storage.
lessons.example: Leftovers need an internal temperature of 74°C.
steps: Choose a suitable container and reheating method.
Heat evenly; stir during microwave reheating.

lessons.whyItWorks: Even heating and an internal check address cold areas in the food.

units.title: Care for clothes and your space
units.goal: Read care instructions and choose a manageable laundry or cleaning plan.
units.why: A few label checks can protect your clothes and your space. You do not have to solve the whole house at once.

lessons.title: The label decides the method
lessons.body: Read how to wash and how to dry. They are separate instructions. Sort items by compatible care needs. Plan the cost and time. Start with one load you know how to handle.
lessons.whyItWorks: Two clothes of the same colour can need different care. The practice table supplies words; a real label may use symbols. Check both the item and machine before using them. A laundry budget includes the whole task, and the time estimate needs room for changing machines or waiting.
lessons.example: Fictional plan: a shirt says cold machine wash and low-heat drying. A wash is CAD 3 for 30 minutes; drying is CAD 2 for 40 minutes.
steps: Choose the cold wash and low-heat dryer setting for this shirt, following the actual machine instructions.
One wash-and-dry task costs $3+2=5$ dollars. Two such tasks would cost $2\times5=10$ dollars.
The cycles take $30+40=70$ minutes. In a 90-minute plan, $90-70=20$ minutes remain for moving items or waiting; queues can still change the plan.
lessons.watchFor: Do not assume all items in one basket can share the hottest or fastest setting. A drying instruction matters too.

lessons.title: A changed label changes the plan
lessons.body: A hand-wash sweater is mixed into the basket. Take it out of the machine load. An unlabelled bottle is nearby. Leave it alone. Choose a known, suitable product for a small cleaning task.
lessons.whyItWorks: Changing one item can change which method is suitable. Dry flat means lay the item flat to dry; it does not mean use a hot dryer. For cleaning, more product or a mixture is not a shortcut. Read the actual instructions and keep the task small enough to finish without rushing.
lessons.example: Fictional change: the sweater says hand wash and dry flat. The bottle by the sink has no label.
steps: Separate the sweater and plan its stated hand-wash and flat-dry method. Ask for help if the method is unfamiliar.
Do not use or mix the unknown liquid. For the table, use a suitable labelled cleaner according to its instructions.
The planned shirt load still costs CAD 5. From CAD 12, $12-5=7$ dollars remain. Check any separate sweater cost rather than inventing one.
lessons.watchFor: Never mix cleaners or transfer them into a drink bottle. A missing label is a reason to stop and check, not guess.

review: Do not assume all items in one basket can share the hottest or fastest setting. A drying instruction matters too.
Never mix cleaners or transfer them into a drink bottle. A missing label is a reason to stop and check, not guess.
State what you know, what you need to check, and who can help.

steps: Pick one manageable task. Read the garment’s care label and the machine’s instructions; ask about a symbol you do not recognise. The linked Canadian symbol guide is an explanation resource, not a claim that every item uses the same label.

For cleaning, choose a suitable product and follow its label, including ventilation and protection. Never mix household chemical products. Keep them in their labelled original containers, closed and out of reach of children and pets.

If a label is missing or a task is unclear, pause and get suitable help or another labelled product. If someone may have been harmed by a chemical, use the poison-centre or medical-help route on Health Canada’s page promptly. Do not wait for an app reply.

units.subject: life
units.title: Protect your time and privacy
units.goal: State a limit, respect another person’s choice and handle pressure.
units.why: You can care about someone and still have a limit. Practise clear words and a backup step without sharing a personal story.

lessons.title: Say what you can do
lessons.body: A limit says what you will do or allow. Keep it clear. You can say no. An offer to help for a short time does not promise the whole evening.
lessons.whyItWorks: A clear boundary describes your own time, belongings or actions. It is different from controlling all of someone else’s choices. “I can stay until six” gives usable information. “You must never ask anyone else” tries to control the other person. A useful limit also leaves room for the other person to decline your offer.
lessons.example: Ari can help Jo with a form until 6:00, but Jo asks Ari to stay until 7:00.
steps: Ari’s limit is leaving at 6:00. Jo’s request does not change it by itself.
Ari can say: I can help until six. I cannot stay later.
Ari may offer another time if it is wanted and workable. Jo does not have to accept that offer.
lessons.watchFor: A clear sentence can help, but it cannot guarantee how someone else will respond.

lessons.title: Keep the limit when the request changes
lessons.body: A new request needs a new choice. You can refuse to share a password even if you agreed to help with a form. If pressure feels unsafe, focus on getting support.
lessons.whyItWorks: Agreeing to one thing is not permission for everything else. Separate the original offer from the new request. You do not have to keep arguing to make a limit valid. If someone ignores it or the situation feels unsafe, a trusted person or support service can help plan a safer next step; the other person’s behaviour is not your fault.
lessons.example: Jo now asks for Ari’s account password so Jo can keep using the form service later.
steps: Ari separates helping with the form from giving account access.
Ari can say: I do not share passwords. I can show you where to start your own account.
If Jo keeps pressuring Ari, Ari can stop the exchange when safe and ask a trusted person for help. Ari need not prove the limit by confronting Jo.
lessons.watchFor: Helping, sharing a device and sharing an account password are different choices.
