units.title: Plan an appointment
units.goal: Read the booking details, plan the time and ask a clear question.
units.why: An appointment has several moving parts. A short plan helps you get there, say what you need and know what happens next.

lessons.title: Work back from check-in
lessons.body: Read the day, time and place. Check-in can be earlier than the visit. Work back from check-in to find when to leave. Use the clinic’s message, not a guess.
lessons.whyItWorks: A start time and an arrival time do different jobs. Work backwards from the requested arrival: subtract the whole journey, including the walk. This gives a latest departure for the stated journey; real delays may need more room. A request for a booking is not yet a confirmed booking.
lessons.example: Fictional visit: Tuesday at 10:30 a.m.; check in at 10:15. Travel takes 25 minutes riding and 5 minutes walking.
steps: Total travel is $25+5=30$ minutes.
Thirty minutes before 10:15 is 9:45 a.m. That is the latest departure for these stated times.
Confirm the place and what to bring. Add room for delays when planning a real trip.
lessons.watchFor: The appointment time is not always the time you should reach the door.

lessons.title: Confirm the change and next step
lessons.body: A changed time or phone visit needs a new plan. Ask what is agreed. Before a visit ends, say the next step back in your own words. Ask again if it is unclear.
lessons.whyItWorks: Repeating a plan exposes gaps: who will call, at what time, and what should happen if the call is missed? A private place and a working phone may matter. If the new plan will not work, ask about alternatives rather than quietly treating an unconfirmed option as settled.
lessons.example: The clinic offers a phone visit at 11:00 a.m. Kai has class then and cannot speak privately.
steps: Kai explains the clash without giving health details in a public message.
Kai asks for another time and asks who will call whom. The offered change stays pending until confirmed.
After the visit, Kai asks: What do I do next, by when, and who do I contact if I am unsure?
lessons.watchFor: A learning plan cannot assess symptoms. Use the appropriate care service; immediate danger needs emergency help.

units.goal: Choose the right health-card route and prepare a question for help.
units.why: A move or lost card is easier to handle when you know which job you are trying to do. Practise with a fictional person first.

lessons.title: Name the job first
lessons.body: A health card connects you with health coverage. First registration, changing details and replacing a lost card are different jobs. Read the situation before choosing a form.
lessons.whyItWorks: A service page may offer several routes. Match the verb to the job: register, update or replace. Eligibility means meeting the service’s conditions. Living in Manitoba is one part of the coverage rules; the official eligibility page covers status and residence conditions too.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Kai moves to Manitoba and has never had Manitoba coverage.
steps: Kai needs to check first-time registration, not merely replace an existing Manitoba card.
Kai reads the eligibility page and the document requirements linked from registration.

lessons.watchFor: A finished practice lesson is not an application or a decision about coverage.

lessons.title: Make the next step possible
lessons.body: A missing card, document or internet connection changes the plan. Ask about the missing piece. Manitoba Health lists help and public-computer options. A saved practice answer is not a submitted form.
lessons.whyItWorks: A checklist separates what you have from what you still need to check. That prevents a guess from becoming a false answer on a form. Manitoba Health asks for relevant changes within 30 days. If you are late or unsure, contact the service rather than assume there is nothing you can do.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Jo moved within Manitoba and cannot find the old card.
steps: Jo already had Manitoba coverage, so this is not simply a first registration.
Jo asks which update and replacement steps fit both the move and the missing card.

units.why: Photo ID can help you prove who you are. Reading the document list and planning the visit can save a wasted trip.

lessons.title: Match the card to the job
lessons.body: The optional Manitoba Identification Card is for people without a driver’s licence. It proves identity; it does not let you drive. MPI checks eligibility and supporting documents.
lessons.whyItWorks: Different cards serve different purposes. The card name alone does not tell you all its rules. Under 18, MPI’s application page says a parent must co-sign. If getting documents or a signature is difficult, ask MPI about your situation before planning a visit; do not assume any adult can sign.

steps: Alex reads the Identification Card page instead of choosing a driving test.

lessons.watchFor: A Manitoba Identification Card is not permission to drive and is not a passport.

lessons.title: Check the combination before the trip
lessons.body: MPI asks for original supporting documents and a specific combination of identity details. The address evidence has date rules. One official-looking document does not automatically cover every requirement.
lessons.whyItWorks: A document can prove one fact but leave another unproved. MPI’s identity page has combination rules, including special rules when using a new plastic health card. A guarantor declaration may help in some situations, but is not a universal substitute. Check the exact combination with MPI rather than improvising it.

units.subject: life

units.goal: Find the right SIN route and protect the number.
units.why: A Social Insurance Number is used for work and government programs. Practise preparing for it and spotting requests that do not need it.

lessons.title: Pick the route for the person
lessons.body: Service Canada handles SINs. Its tool asks who is applying, their status in Canada and how they want to apply. Status means their citizenship or immigration category. Different choices can require different documents.
lessons.whyItWorks: The application path depends on the person and method, not just the document’s name. From age 12, a person can apply for their own SIN. A parent or legal guardian can apply for a minor. Online, mail and in-person routes have format requirements; the tool helps choose the applicable list.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Mo is 16, a Canadian citizen, and wants to apply in person.
steps: Mo selects applying for themself, Canadian citizen and in person on the official tool.
Mo checks the listed primary and secondary identity documents. Primary proves status; secondary confirms identity.
Mo checks the required originals and asks Service Canada about any missing item. Mo does not paste document details into this lesson.
lessons.watchFor: Do not choose a different status merely because its document list looks easier.

lessons.title: Check the request before sharing
lessons.body: A SIN is private. It is not general photo ID. Service Canada says you do not need to give it for a job application. After hiring, payroll has a different reason to need it.
lessons.whyItWorks: A request that sounds official still needs checking. Ask why the number is needed and use a known contact route. A missing confirmation letter does not mean you should seek a different number. The official SIN pages explain how to confirm an existing record. Practise with words such as “my number”, never a real number here.
lessons.example: Fictional case: a stranger asks Mo to send a SIN in a public job-application comment.
steps: Mo does not post the number. An application is not the same stage as hired payroll.
Mo checks the employer through a separate, known contact method.

units.why: A low monthly fee can still come with extra costs. Learn to spot them before you agree.

lessons.title: Compare the whole cost
lessons.body: CAD means Canadian dollars. A bank account holds money. A chequing account is often used for everyday payments. A transaction is one action, such as a payment. Compare the monthly fee and the extra charges together.
lessons.whyItWorks: Compare the same month and the same use. A package may include some transactions and charge for more. Access matters too: an account is less useful if you cannot use its cash machines or get the help you need. The cheapest headline price does not settle every choice.
lessons.example: Made-up offers: A costs CAD 5 a month and includes 10 payments. Each extra payment costs CAD 2. B costs CAD 9 and includes 20. Lee makes 15.
steps: A has $15-10=5$ extra payments. Its cost is $5+5\times2=15$ CAD.
B includes all 15 payments, so its cost is 9 CAD. B is $15-9=6$ CAD cheaper for this use.
Check that the needed payments and access are included. These are fictional offers, not advertised accounts.
lessons.watchFor: A low monthly fee does not mean every service is free.

lessons.title: Check the conditions before agreeing
lessons.body: An offer may depend on age, student status or a minimum balance. Ask what happens when that condition changes. Check the ID and permission requirements with the institution. Do not guess them.
lessons.whyItWorks: The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) lists low-cost and no-cost options, including eligibility for people aged 18 or younger and students at participating institutions. Extra services can still cost money. A fee waiver means a fee is removed only while its conditions hold. Bank access and youth-account arrangements need separate checking; do not assume a parent is available.
lessons.example: New made-up detail: B costs CAD 9 only while Lee is a student. Later it costs CAD 16. Lee’s student status ends soon.
steps: For the same 15 payments, A still costs 15 CAD. After the discount ends, B costs 16 CAD.
Now B costs $16-15=1$ CAD more. The earlier choice needs another look.
Lee asks when the change starts, which no-cost options apply, and which ID and consent arrangements are accepted.
lessons.watchFor: Opening a deposit account is not the same as being approved for a loan or credit card.

units.why: A trip is more than the time spent on the bus. See the walking, waiting and fare together.

lessons.title: Arrive at the door, not just the stop
lessons.body: A timetable lists when buses leave or arrive. Read one row at a time. Check the day and direction. Add the walk from the last stop to the place you need. Leave some spare time.
lessons.whyItWorks: Leaving later is useful only if the whole trip still fits. Count walking and waiting as well as riding. A route number alone does not tell you the direction. Real schedules can change, so the practice table cannot replace a current trip plan. You can choose more walking time or ask for support.
lessons.example: Fictional plan: Kim needs to reach an office by 9 am. The walk from Library stop takes 8 minutes. Bus A arrives at 8:40; B at 8:55; C at 9:10.
steps: A reaches the office at 8:48 am after the walk. That leaves 12 minutes before 9 am.
B reaches it at 9:03 am. Reaching the bus stop before 9 does not make the full trip on time.
Choose A from these options. If walking to its departure stop takes 7 minutes and Kim wants 5 minutes spare, allow $7+5=12$ minutes before its 8:10 departure: leave at 7:58 am.
lessons.watchFor: A scheduled arrival is an estimate, not a promise. Include a margin and check current information.

lessons.title: Replan when the appointment moves
lessons.body: CAD means Canadian dollars. Budget for getting home too. Check which fare or pass fits you. If the appointment changes, compare the whole trip again. A plan that worked yesterday may not work today.
lessons.whyItWorks: Use the same destination and walking time when comparing buses. Keep the fare calculation separate from real eligibility: the price in a maths task is not a current fare quote. Winnipeg’s fare page includes youth-pass and lower-income options with conditions. Having a phone does not mean having data or enough battery; keep a usable backup.
lessons.example: Kim’s appointment moves to 8:45 am. A new fictional option reaches Library at 8:20. Kim has CAD 8; the made-up fare is CAD 3 each way, with no pass or valid return transfer in this case.
steps: The earlier option reaches the office at 8:28 am. Bus A still reaches it at 8:48, three minutes too late.
Two separate fares cost $3+3=6$ CAD. From 8 CAD, $8-6=2$ CAD remains.
Revise the departure time, check a return option and save the route privately. For a real journey, check current fares, access needs and service changes.
lessons.watchFor: Do not spend the return fare just because the first bus has been paid for.

units.subject: life
units.title: Handle a missed connection
units.goal: Recheck the time and fare, then send a clear update when a journey changes.
units.why: Missing a bus is a problem to solve, not a reason to panic or take an unsafe shortcut.

lessons.title: A connection needs time between buses
lessons.body: A connection means changing buses. You may need to walk to another stop. Count that walk before counting spare minutes. A short gap can disappear if the first bus is late.
lessons.whyItWorks: Separate three times: first arrival, reaching the next stop, and the next departure. This prevents counting the same minutes twice. A transfer is also a fare rule, not a promise that the bus will wait. Winnipeg’s current guidance gives transfers a time limit; check the actual expiry and payment method.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Max reaches Hub at 9:12 am and needs 4 minutes to reach the next stop. The Tight bus leaves at 9:18; Later leaves at 9:30. After Centre, Max needs a 5-minute walk for a 10 am appointment.
steps: Max reaches the next stop at 9:16 am. The Tight bus leaves just 2 minutes later.
Later leaves 14 minutes after Max reaches that stop. It gets to Centre at 9:50; the final walk reaches the appointment at 9:55.
Later offers a larger connection margin and still fits this appointment. Check real conditions before choosing; a margin cannot prevent every delay.
lessons.watchFor: The gap between bus times is not all waiting time if you must walk between stops.

lessons.title: Say what changed and what you know
lessons.body: Pause in a safe place. Recheck the trip from where you are now. A saved timetable is useful, but it may be out of date. Keep an estimate separate from a confirmed fact.
lessons.whyItWorks: If the connection no longer works, compare the next safe option with the appointment and return needs. A clear update says what happened, the new estimated arrival and a question. Transfer expiry may also change the cost. A missed connection does not guarantee a free extra ride; use official information or ask.
lessons.example: The first bus is delayed to 9:26 am. The 4-minute walk now ends at 9:30, exactly when Later is due to leave. Next leaves at 9:45 and gets to Centre at 10:05.
steps: Do not count a zero-minute margin as a reliable connection or run into traffic. Recheck live information and the next workable option.
Next plus the 5-minute walk gives 10:10 am, an estimated 10 minutes late. Ask whether the appointment can still go ahead.
In this made-up case, the printed transfer ends at 9:40. Boarding at 9:45 would be 5 minutes later. Check the payment needed and keep the return plan workable.
lessons.watchFor: A saved message in Stepstone has not been sent. Use a real agreed contact method when travelling.

lessons.title: Build the plan before booking
lessons.body: MPI means Manitoba Public Insurance. A Class 5 licence is the usual passenger-vehicle licence. CAD means Canadian dollars. Start with the official route, documents and study plan. Passing Stepstone does not give permission to drive.
lessons.whyItWorks: A first Manitoba licence normally starts at 16; the age-15-and-a-half route needs an eligible Driver Z course in progress. Under-18 applicants need the required consent. Registration, knowledge testing, vision and medical standards, and licence issue are separate steps. MPI offers knowledge-test audio; ask about other access needs before booking. A missing requirement is a question to resolve, not something to fake.
lessons.example: Fictional Noor is 17 and planning the first steps. The savings goal for now is CAD 90, with CAD 68 saved. This is a made-up goal, not a quote for a licence or its total cost.
steps: Use MPI’s route to list ID, consent and testing questions. Keep real documents private.
The savings gap is $90-68=22$ CAD. Check actual fees and other costs before treating the goal as enough.
Plan short handbook study sessions. Four sessions of 15 minutes give $4\times15=60$ minutes. Study time helps learning but does not certify readiness.
lessons.watchFor: The knowledge test, road test, licence and any lessons can have separate costs. Check the current full plan.

lessons.title: Practice needs the right support
lessons.body: New drivers move through Learner, Intermediate and Full stages. Each has rules. A friend willing to sit beside you is not automatically a qualified supervising driver. Check the whole arrangement before driving.
lessons.whyItWorks: The Learner stage has a nine-month minimum; passing the road test leads to an Intermediate stage with a fifteen-month minimum. Licence validity and other conditions matter. Learners need a qualified supervisor: a valid minimum Class 5 Full licence held for at least three years, the only front-seat passenger, and compliance with MPI’s alcohol and drug rules. Learner alcohol and drug restrictions also apply. Read the complete current rules.
lessons.example: Noor later has a Learner licence. A cousin offers to supervise but has held a Full licence for only two years. Noor still needs transport to work.
steps: Check the supervisor requirements. This cousin does not meet the three-year Full-stage requirement, even if Noor feels confident.
Look for a qualified arrangement or ask about permitted driving-school options. Do not drive alone to practise.
Revise the plan: keep studying and use a workable bus or other travel option meanwhile. Completing minimum time does not replace the required test or prove practical skill.
lessons.watchFor: A practice score does not change licence restrictions or authorize a vehicle, supervisor or road test.

steps: Check MPI’s Class 5 route for your situation, age and any required consent. Register with accepted identification before booking. Ask MPI about missing documents, unavailable required support or access needs; do not invent a signature.

units.subject: life
units.title: Read road signs
units.goal: Connect a sign to its meaning, then check the time, conditions and people around it.
units.why: Reading a shape or number is the start. Understanding when the instruction applies is the useful part.

lessons.title: Read the shape and the details
lessons.body: A red eight-sided STOP sign requires a complete stop. A downward-pointing yield triangle means give way: slow down and stop if needed. Some signs also use days and times. Read those details as part of the message.
lessons.whyItWorks: Shape helps recognition, but one feature is not the whole rule. A 24-hour clock numbers the hours from midnight. Before noon the hour matches am time. For 13 through 23, subtract 12 to get the pm hour. Keep the minutes. Noon is 12:00; midnight is 00:00. Connect the sign to the handbook rule, not just a colour.
lessons.example: Study example: compare a STOP sign with a yield sign, then read a separate posted time of 17:30.
steps: Name the difference: STOP requires stopping; yield requires giving way, with a stop when needed.
For 17:30, $17-12=5$, so the time is 5:30 pm. The 30 minutes stay the same.
Find the full sign or rule in the handbook. A single recognised shape does not mean every driving situation is understood.
lessons.watchFor: Yield does not mean “keep moving no matter what.” Colour alone is not a complete instruction.

lessons.title: A condition changes when a rule applies
lessons.body: A condition is a detail that must be true. A sign may name an action, days and times. Read them together. People crossing, traffic signals and other rules still matter even when one posted restriction is not active.
lessons.whyItWorks: Think through the whole message instead of stopping at one number. A weekday-only time window needs both the correct day and time. Outside that window, only that timed restriction stops applying; other rules can still prevent the action. At a pedestrian signal, an orange hand means do not begin crossing. Watch for turning traffic and use the actual crossing instructions.
lessons.example: Fictional study sign: no right turn, Monday to Friday, 07:00 to 09:00. First case: Tuesday at 8:20 am. Changed case: Saturday at 8:20 am.
steps: Tuesday is a named day and 8:20 is inside the window, so the posted turn restriction applies.
Saturday is not a named day. That timed restriction is not active, but this alone does not prove a turn is safe or permitted.
Explain what still needs checking: other signs, signals, lane rules and people crossing. Do not use a time calculation as permission to ignore them.
lessons.watchFor: Reading one sign correctly is not the same as assessing the whole road situation.

units.subject: life
units.title: Compare places to live
units.goal: Compare the whole cost of a place and find what you need to ask before agreeing.
units.why: The lowest rent on an advert may not mean the lowest monthly cost. A few good questions can prevent a costly surprise.

lessons.title: Count more than the advertised rent
lessons.body: Rent pays for the place. Utilities are services such as heat or electricity. Some are included; others cost extra. Add the costs for the same month before comparing.
lessons.whyItWorks: A fair comparison includes the same items for both choices. An estimate is a best guess, not a promised bill. Keep money for food and other needs separate. A lower total only helps if the place, location and terms also work for the person.
lessons.example: Cedar costs 760 dollars rent, 90 energy and 70 travel each month. Birch costs 820 rent, includes energy and adds 50 travel. The monthly limit is 900 dollars.
steps: Cedar totals 760 + 90 + 70 = 920 dollars a month.
Birch totals 820 + 0 + 50 = 870 dollars a month.
Only Birch fits the stated 900-dollar limit; a lower rent alone did not make Cedar cheaper overall.
lessons.watchFor: Do not compare one place’s rent alone with another place’s total. Keep the time period and included items the same.

lessons.title: Read what you would be agreeing to
lessons.body: A lease is a rental agreement. Read what it includes. Moving in can also need a deposit and other costs. If a detail changes, stop and update your plan before agreeing.
lessons.whyItWorks: Monthly costs and move-in money answer different questions. In an ordinary Manitoba tenancy covered by RTB rules, a security deposit is limited to half the first month’s rent; ask RTB about other deposits or situations. A spoken promise about an included service should be clarified in the agreement. Check the terms, not just the total.
lessons.example: Birch’s first rent is 820 dollars and its stated deposit is 410 dollars. There are 1180 dollars available for those two payments.
steps: The first rent and deposit total 820 + 410 = 1230 dollars.
The shortfall is 1230 − 1180 = 50 dollars; that is separate from the recurring monthly comparison.
Before committing, confirm what is included and every required payment. If energy is later billed separately, recalculate the monthly total too.
lessons.watchFor: Do not add the deposit to every month’s rent. Do not assume a lower advertised rent, a possible benefit or a verbal promise solves a shortfall.

review: Rent pays for the place. Utilities are services such as heat or electricity. Some are included; others cost extra. Add the costs for the same month before comparing.
A lease is a rental agreement. Read what it includes. Moving in can also need a deposit and other costs. If a detail changes, stop and update your plan before agreeing.

steps: For a real place, check the rent, due date, length of the agreement, named tenants and included services. Ask for unclear terms to be explained before agreeing. Check who you are dealing with before sending money.

Plan monthly spending separately from money needed to move in. Confirm deposits, receipts and the condition of the place. RTB can explain which rules apply, including questions about shared housing or renting while under 18.

If the cost does not fit, ask about other housing or support. Rent Assist has conditions to check; a lesson score does not make someone eligible. Keep real agreements, receipts and addresses out of Stepstone.

units.subject: life
units.title: Keep track of home bills
units.goal: Read a bill, plan payment dates and ask early when the money will not cover it.
units.why: A bill has several numbers. Knowing which is the total, and when it is due, helps you make a useful plan.

lessons.title: Find the total without counting it twice
lessons.body: A balance is money still owed. New charges add to it. Payments already counted reduce it. The amount due is the result. Find the due date, then check when your money is available.
lessons.whyItWorks: A statement’s total often already includes the other lines. Adding them again makes a false debt. Also separate a bill’s issue date from its payment deadline. Having enough money next week does not mean it is available for a bill due today. A calendar makes that timing visible.
lessons.example: Fictional energy bill: CAD 30 unpaid, CAD 90 new charges and CAD 20 already credited. Internet adds CAD 45 on a different date.
steps: Energy: $30+90-20=100$ dollars due. Do not add the CAD 100 total to its own parts.
Both bills need $100+45=145$ dollars. With CAD 130 available, the gap is $145-130=15$ dollars.
Energy is due 15 October and internet on 18 October. The stated pay date, 20 October, comes after both deadlines. Ask about the gap early.
lessons.watchFor: The bill date is not necessarily the due date. A future pay date or a reminder does not automatically extend a deadline.

lessons.title: Ask, confirm, then update the calendar
lessons.body: If money is short, contact the provider. Explain the problem and ask about options. A payment plan is only agreed when the provider confirms it. Keep the amount and date for each part.
lessons.whyItWorks: A partial payment leaves a balance. It does not create an extension by itself. In the fictional example, a provider confirms new dates; that confirmation is the reason the calendar changes. Check future commitments too. An equal-payment plan spreads costs; it does not make energy free or erase an old balance.
lessons.example: Fictional change: energy payments are confirmed as CAD 40 on 15 October and CAD 60 on 22 October. Internet stays CAD 45 on 18 October.
steps: By 18 October, the plan needs $40+45=85$ dollars. CAD 130 available leaves $130-85=45$ dollars for this plan.
The remaining energy part is CAD 60, so the stated CAD 45 alone is $60-45=15$ dollars short. Confirm money available before 22 October.
Record the provider’s confirmation and both dates. If the later money will not arrive, contact the provider again; do not silently assume another extension.
lessons.watchFor: Treat an unexpected payment message cautiously. Open the known provider’s site or number yourself, rather than using an urgent message’s link.

review: The bill date is not necessarily the due date. A future pay date or a reminder does not automatically extend a deadline.
Treat an unexpected payment message cautiously. Open the known provider’s site or number yourself, rather than using an urgent message’s link.
State what you know, what you need to check, and who can help.
units.reflection: Explain Ari’s revised dates, the money still needed and how to tell a request from a confirmed arrangement.

steps: Use the provider’s official account or contact route. Check the period, payments already credited, amount due and due date. Ask about a charge you do not understand; keep real records private.
Set a reminder and use an accepted payment method early enough for it to arrive. A saved reminder or pending transfer is not proof that a bill is paid. Check the receipt and provider balance.

If you cannot pay in full, contact the provider promptly. Manitoba Hydro lists payment arrangements and help programs with conditions. Ask what is agreed, record the dates, and follow up if the plan changes. No lesson can promise a fee waiver or funding.

units.subject: life
units.title: Ask for a home repair
units.goal: Describe a problem clearly, keep a useful record and follow up through the right route.
units.why: You do not have to diagnose a fault to explain what you noticed and ask for it to be checked.

lessons.title: Describe what happened, not a guessed cause
lessons.body: A useful repair request says where, what and when. Describe what you noticed. Ask for a next step. Keep a copy. You can be clear without knowing the technical name or blaming anyone.
lessons.whyItWorks: An observation is something you actually noticed. A diagnosis explains the cause, which may need a qualified person. Keeping those separate makes a request more accurate. A dated record helps follow-up, but a sent message does not prove it was read or the repair completed.
lessons.example: Fictional case: a kitchen cupboard door hangs loose on Monday at 6 pm. The written request is sent at 6:15 pm. A reply proposes Wednesday, 2–4 pm.
steps: Record the location and observation: “The kitchen cupboard door hangs loose.” Do not invent the cause.
Write when it was noticed and ask when it can be checked. The gap between 6:00 and 6:15 is 15 minutes.
The proposed visit lasts $4-2=2$ hours. Keep the reply and clarify access using the applicable rules; an appointment offer is not a completed repair.
lessons.watchFor: A repair note is not a reason to try electrical, gas or other unfamiliar repair work. This practice case is an ordinary non-emergency request.

lessons.title: Follow up when the plan changes
lessons.body: A work shift now overlaps the visit. Ask about another time and get confirmation. Keep the problem and dates clear. If repairs remain unresolved, ask the tenancy service about the next step.
lessons.whyItWorks: The new availability does not silently cancel an agreed or lawfully notified visit. Communicate and clarify access. For unresolved ordinary repairs, RTB has a formal request route; do not hold back rent on your own. A new immediate danger changes the route entirely: leave danger and use the proper emergency service, rather than waiting for the mentor.
lessons.example: Fictional change: Wednesday work is 2–5 pm. Thursday class is 10 am–noon. The offered alternatives are Thursday 9–11 am and Friday 1–3 pm.
steps: Wednesday overlaps work. Thursday’s proposed visit overlaps class between 10 and 11 am.
Friday 1–3 pm has no conflict in the stated schedule. Ask to use it and wait for confirmation; it is a proposal until agreed.
Update the record after the visit with what was actually done. If the needed repair is still unresolved, ask RTB about the appropriate next step using the saved facts.
lessons.watchFor: Do not treat any fixed number of days in a practice calculation as a legal repair deadline. Urgency and circumstances affect the proper response.

review: A repair note is not a reason to try electrical, gas or other unfamiliar repair work. This practice case is an ordinary non-emergency request.
Do not treat any fixed number of days in a practice calculation as a legal repair deadline. Urgency and circumstances affect the proper response.
State what you know, what you need to check, and who can help.

steps: For an ordinary rental repair, tell the landlord what needs attention, preferably in writing. State where it is, what you observed and when. Keep a private record of the request and response.

If needed repairs are not addressed, use the Residential Tenancies Branch’s repair information and ask which formal route applies. Follow lawful access arrangements. Do not withhold rent on your own to force a repair.

An urgent danger needs the proper immediate route, not an ordinary app report. For a suspected gas leak or sounding CO alarm, leave the area and call 911 or local emergency services from safety. Use the official emergency guidance; never attempt a repair based on this lesson.

units.subject: life
units.title: Get ready to file taxes
units.goal: Sort the right records and choose a workable way to file a return.
units.why: Taxes feel less mysterious when you separate the papers, the choices and the next small step.

lessons.title: A tax return puts the year together
lessons.body: A return is the information you send the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) about a tax year. CAD means Canadian dollars. A refund is money returned after the calculation. A T4 is an employer’s yearly slip. It is different from one payday’s payslip.
lessons.whyItWorks: Read the labels before doing arithmetic. T4 box 14 reports employment income; box 22 reports income tax already deducted. A deduction reduces income used in the tax calculation. A tax credit reduces tax, under its own rules. Neither word means every expense is refunded. The full return can include other income and claims.
lessons.example: Fictional records for one year: Lee has two different jobs. T4 A box 14: CAD 6,000; box 22: CAD 150. T4 B box 14: CAD 4,000; box 22: CAD 100.
steps: Match the person, tax year and employer. The two slips cover different jobs, not duplicate copies.
For these records, employment income totals $6000+4000=10000$ CAD. Tax already deducted totals $150+100=250$ CAD.
Keep those labels separate. These two totals alone do not calculate Lee’s refund or final tax.
lessons.watchFor: Do not count a downloaded copy and a mailed copy of the same slip as two incomes.

lessons.title: Choose help and handle a missing slip
lessons.body: You can file with certified software, on paper, or with suitable help. A free clinic may help people with modest income and a simple situation. Ask about eligibility, access and what to bring.
lessons.whyItWorks: Preparing, saving and sending are separate steps. Choose the right tax year and provincial package, then check current filing and payment dates. If a slip is missing, ask its issuer. CRA also explains what to do if it cannot arrive in time. A missing slip is not a reason to hide income or guess a number from memory.
lessons.example: Fictional change: Lee has only a phone and is still missing the second employer’s slip.
steps: Lee asks that employer for the correct year’s slip and gathers the available pay records.
Lee asks a clinic whether the situation fits and whether phone, in-person or other help is available.
Lee checks the real deadlines and missing-slip instructions. After filing, Lee keeps the confirmation and supporting records privately.
lessons.watchFor: Saving a draft in software or Stepstone does not mean CRA received a return.

review: Do not count a downloaded copy and a mailed copy of the same slip as two incomes.
Saving a draft in software or Stepstone does not mean CRA received a return.
State what you know, what you need to check, and who can help.
units.reflection: Using Lee’s fictional case, explain the revised filing plan and why a missing slip does not mean missing income.

steps: Open CRA’s preparation page. Check the tax year, who should file, and both the filing and payment dates for the person’s situation.
Gather that year’s income records and relevant receipts privately. Compare slips by issuer and year; request missing or corrected records. Use CRA’s missing-slip guidance if time is short.

Choose certified tax software, paper, or suitable help from CRA’s filing page. A free clinic may fit a modest income and simple situation; ask the clinic first. Review the return, send it through that route and keep the confirmation.

lessons.title: Refund, owing or zero?
lessons.body: The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) sends a notice of assessment after processing a return. CAD means Canadian dollars. A refund means money back. A balance owing means money to pay. Nil means zero. Read the words beside the amount, not just the number.
lessons.whyItWorks: Compare the total payable with total credits. Payable is the calculated amount charged; credits include amounts already paid or deducted and other applicable credits. More credits than payable can give a refund. Fewer can leave a balance owing. We use supplied totals here, not a formula for calculating anyone’s real tax.
lessons.example: Fictional teaching summary: total payable CAD 400; total credits CAD 650. No other balance or adjustment is included in this example.
steps: Credits exceed payable. The difference is $650-400=250$ CAD back in this example.
If payable were 700 CAD with the same 650 CAD credits, $700-650=50$ CAD would be owing.
If both were 650 CAD, the difference would be zero. Real notices may also show other balances or changes.
lessons.watchFor: A refund is not your total yearly pay, and tax already deducted is not automatically the final tax bill.

lessons.title: Read the change and choose an action
lessons.body: Check the year, amount and explanation on the notice. If something is wrong, use the official correction route. If you cannot pay, ask CRA about arrangements. Do not ignore a letter you do not understand.
lessons.whyItWorks: A question can be specific without exposing documents in this app. Name the line or change and ask what evidence is needed. For a change to your filed information, wait for the notice of assessment and use CRA’s change-return process. Keep records. Benefits have their own conditions and notices; yearly filing can matter even when there is little or no income.
lessons.example: Fictional change: Ren expected CAD 250 back. The notice now says CAD 40 owing and explains that a claimed credit was not allowed.
steps: Ren compares the explanation with the return and supporting records. A different result is a reason to investigate, not proof that Ren did something dishonest.
Ren asks CRA which evidence or correction route fits. If Ren cannot pay, Ren asks about a payment arrangement; a plan in this app is not an agreement with CRA.
Ren keeps the documents and separately checks benefit information. Ren does not budget a benefit just because a quiz or return is complete.
lessons.watchFor: A payment arrangement is not automatic debt cancellation. Check current terms and any interest that continues.

lessons.title: Match the help to the job
lessons.body: Start with the need: I need help filling in a form. Then check who the service helps, what it costs and how to reach it. A familiar name is not enough.
lessons.whyItWorks: A service can be real and still be wrong for this job. Compare the need with the service’s purpose, age rules, cost and booking method. A listed opening time is not a promise of a free place. Ask the service about availability and requirements.
lessons.example: Fictional case: Rae is 17 and wants free help with a form after 4:00 p.m.

lessons.title: Make a backup without oversharing
lessons.body: If the first route is full or closed, ask for another. Give the details needed for the next step. Before sharing private information, ask who can see it and why it is needed.
lessons.whyItWorks: A useful request names the job and the obstacle. “I need form help, but that session is full” gives a helper something specific to work with. Privacy rules differ between services and contact methods, and can have exceptions. Ask rather than assume total secrecy or post documents publicly.

lessons.title: Agree on a clear turn-taking plan.
lessons.body: When two people need the same tool, agree who uses it first and how it passes to the next person. Check the real time limit for both tasks.
lessons.example: Two people share one tablet for a practice activity.
steps: Agree that each person completes one round.
Use a written order or visible marker.
Save work and switch accounts before handing the tablet over.
lessons.whyItWorks: Shared tasks need a clear handoff. Agree on who does which part, how long a turn lasts if relevant, and how someone signals they are ready. A turn can involve speaking, using equipment, or making a decision. The useful rule is one everyone can understand and use, not simply who speaks the loudest.
lessons.watchFor: Silence is not a reliable agreement to a new responsibility.

lessons.title: Repair a mix-up directly
lessons.body: If the plan stops working, say what changed and agree a new handoff. Do not assume the other person can guess your timing or that silence means agreement.
lessons.example: Work through the reasoning
steps: State what you noticed without labelling the person.
Check the agreed order.
Choose a clear next turn and make the order visible.
lessons.whyItWorks: When a handoff breaks down, describe the task and ask to reset the agreement. You can request a written order or a clear signal. If someone needs more processing time, a pause can be part of the plan. Taking turns does not mean accepting an unfair share of work without discussing it.
lessons.watchFor: Equal turns and identical time are not always the same as a workable plan.

review: When two people need the same tool, agree who uses it first and how it passes to the next person. Check the real time limit for both tasks.

lessons.title: Check before you guess
lessons.body: Two instructions may conflict or leave something out. Name the exact difference. Ask the person responsible which instruction to use before doing work that may need redoing.
lessons.example: Put those boxes over there.
steps: Notice the unclear detail: where?
Ask: Which shelf do you mean?
Check: This shelf, with the labels facing out. Is that right?
lessons.whyItWorks: Confirm the result the instruction is meant to produce, then identify the next action and any missing detail. Repeating the words without understanding the task may hide a misunderstanding. A short restatement lets the other person correct the plan before time or materials are used.
lessons.watchFor: Nodding or saying yes does not itself confirm understanding.

lessons.title: Ask for an example
lessons.body: Say the confirmed plan back in your own words. You can ask for an example or written steps. The useful test is whether you know what to do next.
lessons.example: I understand the goal but not the first step.
steps: Say what you know: I need to sort these.

Ask: Could you show me one example?
lessons.whyItWorks: When instructions conflict, state the conflict factually and ask which priority applies. If a task could be unsafe, stop and get appropriate guidance instead of experimenting with a guess. Asking for clarification can prevent rework; it is part of doing a task carefully.
lessons.watchFor: Do not invent a deadline or safety procedure that was not supplied.

lessons.title: Describe a problem with enough detail to get help.
lessons.body: Say what happened and where. Give the size of the problem if you know it. A specific report helps someone act more than blaming a person.
lessons.example: A document does not print.
steps: Goal: print the named document.

lessons.whyItWorks: Describe the observable problem before assigning a cause or blame. Include the task, what happened, and how it affects the next step. “Three labels are missing, so I cannot match the boxes” gives another person something specific to work with. lessons.title: Agree on the next step

Record the agreed update or check-back time.
lessons.whyItWorks: Offer a reasonable next step or ask who can decide. Separate a temporary workaround from a permanent fix. After action is taken, check whether the original problem is resolved. A clear report can be brief and direct; it does not need exaggerated language to be worth taking seriously.
lessons.watchFor: Saying everything is broken can hide the one detail needed to fix the problem.

lessons.title: Describe the support that helps
lessons.body: An adjustment is a change that helps you do the task. Name the practical need and a support to try. You do not have to share a diagnosis or private family details in this practice.
lessons.example: It is hard to hear the steps in this room.
steps: Name the problem without blaming yourself.
Offer an option: Could you write the steps or explain them somewhere quieter?

lessons.whyItWorks: A useful adjustment changes the task or communication so you can participate more effectively. Identify the barrier and a specific support: written instructions, a quieter place, a demonstration, or a predictable check-in. You can describe the practical need without sharing a diagnosis or personal history.
lessons.watchFor: An adjustment request is not a demand to be treated as incapable.

lessons.title: Give yourself processing time
lessons.body: Try the support on one step. If it still does not help, explain what remains difficult and suggest a change. There can be more than one workable format.
lessons.example: A question comes too quickly.
steps: Say: Give me a moment to think, please.
If needed: Could you ask that another way?
Answer when you understand what is being asked.
lessons.whyItWorks: Check whether the adjustment helps with the actual task. If not, explain what still gets in the way and suggest another approach. Different people may need different supports; there is no single correct preference. This practice is about expressing a need clearly, not deciding legal entitlements or medical treatment.
lessons.watchFor: A support that helps one person may not help another.

lessons.title: Clarify a disagreement before trying to solve it.
lessons.body: Describe the specific issue and ask what the other person needs. A boundary says what you need to keep or protect. You can be clear without guessing their motives.
lessons.example: Two people thought they had the same turn on a shared tool.
steps: State your understanding of the order.
Ask what order the other person understood.
Check the written plan or agree a new visible order.
lessons.whyItWorks: Begin a disagreement by checking what each person means. Two people may share a goal while disagreeing about timing or method. Describe the observable issue and its effect, then ask a specific question. Keep your boundary clear without needing to insult or diagnose the other person.
lessons.watchFor: Understanding another view does not require agreeing with it.

lessons.title: Look for a next step, not a personality verdict
lessons.body: Look for an option that meets the important needs. Confirm it together. If you cannot agree or the issue is outside your role, ask an appropriate person for help.
lessons.example: Work through the reasoning
steps: Name the practical concern.
Suggest two workable options.
Confirm the agreement, or ask an appropriate person to help mediate.
lessons.whyItWorks: A workable resolution names the next action, who owns it, and when to review it. If the conversation becomes threatening, prioritize leaving the situation and seeking appropriate support rather than trying to win the argument. No sample script can guarantee another person’s response; the scenarios show possible outcomes to compare.
lessons.watchFor: You cannot control another person’s reaction by finding one perfect sentence.

review: Describe the specific issue and ask what the other person needs. A boundary says what you need to keep or protect. You can be clear without guessing their motives.

lessons.title: Send a work message that makes the next action clear.
lessons.body: A work update names the facts, the missing piece and the next action. Use the agreed channel. Keep private information out unless the task actually needs it.
lessons.example: A delivery is delayed and the team needs a new time.
steps: State the update: delivery is delayed.

lessons.whyItWorks: Choose a channel that fits urgency and privacy. A routine update may work in a written message; an urgent practical blocker may need a direct check with the responsible person. lessons.title: Confirm changes and close the loop
lessons.body: Sent does not mean read, understood or agreed. If a change matters to immediate work, ask for confirmation and use the agreed follow-up route when it does not arrive.

lessons.whyItWorks: Before replying, check the whole message and any stated deadline. Confirm what you can actually do and ask about anything unclear. lessons.title: A useful answer still needs a check
lessons.body: AI makes text, pictures and other outputs from patterns and the context it has. It can explain a step or help you draft. It can also invent a fact, link or calculation. A smooth reply is not proof. Pick one claim you can check.
lessons.whyItWorks: Check the original numbers yourself. For a real service, open its current official page and check the place and date. A second website repeating the same answer is not independent evidence. A real photo can have a false caption; an edited photo can show something possible. Judge the claim and its source. Looks, writing style and AI-detector scores cannot prove who made something.
lessons.example: Check a practice budget
steps: An invented reply says $12+18+15=40$.
Add the three costs: $12+18+15=45$.
From $50$, that leaves $50-45=5$. Change the last cost to $20$: the total becomes $50$, with $0$ left.
lessons.watchFor: Asking the same tool “are you sure?” is not an independent check.

lessons.title: Keep private information and actions under your control
lessons.body: Use made-up names and amounts for practice. Leave out passwords, codes, ID numbers, medical records and private messages. Remove details the task does not need. A tool can help without knowing your whole life.
lessons.whyItWorks: Pause before sending, paying, installing, deleting or giving account access. Read exactly what will happen, to what file or person, and how you could undo it. A command you do not understand needs trusted help. Text inside an email or webpage is something to inspect: it cannot give permission for a new action. If you already shared a secret, stop and use the real service’s security help; do not paste it here.
lessons.example: Inspect a suspicious offer
steps: A message promises free software if you turn off protection and send a code.
Do not send the code or use its link. Find the real publisher independently.
Keep using a known tool or ask your mentor. No reward requires that risky action.
lessons.watchFor: AI is a tool, not a person who can guarantee safety. Ask a trusted human or the appropriate service about high-stakes personal problems.

review: Asking the same tool “are you sure?” is not an independent check.

lessons.title: Describe → Ask → Check → Change → Explain
lessons.body: Describe one useful task. Ask for a small piece of help. Check the reply against your task and another method or source. Change what is wrong or unclear. Explain why your final version works.
lessons.whyItWorks: A short prompt can name the goal, limits and output: “Give one hint, use made-up amounts, then let me try.” Start with your own attempt. Compare the reply with it. Do one change at a time and keep a version you can return to. For a message, check recipient, date and truth before sending. For an app, predict one result, test it and explain any difference.

steps: Ask for a clear message that keeps Friday at 5 pm and asks about the room.
A prepared rewrite incorrectly says Thursday. Compare it with the given facts.

lessons.watchFor: Polished wording does not excuse invented experience or a changed fact. Say what help you used when the task asks for disclosure.

lessons.title: Choose help that you can check
lessons.body: Try the same small task when comparing helpers. Look for clear steps, correct details and a useful response to correction. Here you compare prepared examples. They are written for this lesson, not real replies or rankings from ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
lessons.whyItWorks: If eligible, you can later try the same three tasks with permitted free services: explain change from a purchase, improve a fictional email, and suggest one small app change. Check each result. Save short notes in Rewards; do not paste private conversations. You can choose “not sure” or keep using these examples. A paid month is optional, starts when your project is ready, and needs secured funding and mentor approval.
lessons.example: Compare prepared replies to a request about a 20-dollar payment for a 7-dollar item.
steps: One reply says 13 dollars change; another says 27 dollars.
Check the task independently: 20 minus 7 is 13, and 7 plus 13 is 20.
Prefer the reply that preserves the facts and allows a check. This one task does not rank a provider for every other job.
lessons.watchFor: No outside account is required to complete these lessons. Under-13 supervised services do not automatically qualify for a paid plan. Learning and the free project continue if no paid option fits.

lessons.title: Join the right network
lessons.body: Wi-Fi connects your device to a nearby network. Ask the person responsible for the network for its exact name. Use the device’s network settings to join.
lessons.example: Library staff give you the guest network name.
steps: The library gives you its guest network name.
Match that exact name in Wi-Fi settings.
Use the library’s instructions, then open its website to check.
lessons.whyItWorks: Signal strength does not establish who operates a network. Check the actual situation before applying the same method to a new task.
lessons.watchFor: A strong signal does not prove who owns the network.

lessons.title: Check a failed connection
lessons.body: A connection problem does not always mean the password is wrong. Check the network name, signal and device settings. Ask for help before changing shared equipment.
lessons.example: A connected device cannot load the library page.
steps: The page does not load.
Check that Wi-Fi is on and the expected network is selected.
If it still fails, ask the library staff for help.
lessons.whyItWorks: A working connection can still reach a website that has a problem. Check the actual situation before applying the same method to a new task.
lessons.watchFor: Ask before resetting equipment that other people use.

Set a reminder early enough to get ready and travel.

lessons.example: The organiser sends a later start time.

Edit the original event to show 3 pm.
Check the reminder and remove an old duplicate if you created one.

steps: A shop job involves stock checks and customer questions.

lessons.title: Find the job requirements
lessons.body: A job posting describes the role and how to apply. Find the duties, hours, location and closing date. Separate required skills from skills the employer would prefer.

steps: The posting says: weekend assistant, city centre, apply by Friday.

Check how the employer wants applications sent.

steps: A preferred skill is listed separately from a required one.

steps: A customer asks where to collect an order.

steps: The required equipment is unavailable.
